item.title: Cluster health
item.description:
Cluster health #

Returns the cluster health for quick overview.

Get the whole cluster health #

Requests # 

GET /_cluster/health

The call is bounded by a 10s timeout; when the cluster cannot answer in time it returns HTTP 503 with "status": "timeout", "timeout": true and points at /_node/_local/recovery for details — treat that as “degraded, still converging” when polling for readiness.

Query Parameters #

  • level
    (Optional, string) Can be one of cluster, regions, collections rollings or shards. Controls the details level of the health information returned. Defaults to cluster.

Get the health of a specific region #

Requests # 

GET /_cluster/_region/<region_id>/health

Path parameters #

  • region_id
    (Required, String) The region to query. Currently only the special ID _local — the region that handles this request — is implemented; a remote region UUID answers 501 not implemented yet.

Query Parameters #

  • level
    (Optional, string) Can be one of regions, collections rollings or shards. Controls the details level of the health information returned. Defaults to regions.

item.title: Concepts
item.description:
Concepts #

Pizza is a distributed search engine designed to efficiently index and retrieve documents across large-scale datasets. It organizes data in a hierarchical structure, allowing for flexible management and retrieval capabilities.

Before you start using Pizza, familiarize yourself with the following key concepts:

[Pizza Concepts]

Concepts #

Cluster #

A cluster represents a set of interconnected nodes that collectively form the Pizza search engine. Nodes within a cluster collaborate to store and process data efficiently. Clusters can span multiple physical locations for fault tolerance and scalability.

item.title: Create a collection
item.description:
Create a collection #

Creates a new collection.

Examples #

The following request creates a new collection called my-collection in the namespace my-namespace:

PUT /my-namespace:my-collection

If creating a collection within the default namespace, it can be simplified as:

PUT /my-collection

Request # 

PUT /[<namespace>:]<name>

Path parameters #

  • <namespace>
    (Optional, string) The namespace which the collection belongs to. Namespace names must meet the following criteria:
    • Lowercase only
    • Cannot include \ /, *, ?, ", <, >, |, , ,, #
    • Cannot start with -, _, +
    • Cannot be . or ..
    • Cannot be longer than 255 bytes (note it is bytes, so multi-byte characters will count towards the 255 limit faster)
  • <name>
    (Required, string) Name of the collection you wish to create. Collection names must meet the same criteria as namespace names.

Query parameters #

item.title: In-place columns for hot counters and flags
item.description:
In-place columns for hot counters and flags #

Fields that change constantly — view counters, stock levels, feature flags, ranking scores — used to pay a full document rebuild on every partial update. Marking a numeric or boolean field with "inplace": true gives it a dedicated typed column instead:

PUT /my-collection
{
 "properties": {
 "title": { "type": "keyword" },
 "views": { "type": "integer", "inplace": true },
 "score": { "type": "double", "inplace": true },
 "active": { "type": "boolean", "inplace": true }
 }
}

Partial updates on such fields become O(1) column writes — no fetch, merge, and re-index of the document. Atomic-style operators work directly against the column:

item.title: List the cluster trash
item.description:
List the cluster trash #

List every node’s trash, merged into one cluster-wide, namespace-centric view. The request may be sent to any node; the node that receives it aggregates the trash of every cluster member.

Examples # 

GET /_cluster/trash

A typical item — here a deleted namespace held on two nodes:

{
 "nodes_scanned": 2,
 "unreachable_nodes": [],
 "retention_secs": 86400,
 "items": [
 {
 "name": "1788916375_namespace-website",
 "deleted_at": 1788916375,
 "bytes": 2097152,
 "files": 42,
 "kind": "namespace",
 "namespace": "website",
 "collections": 3,
 "shard_groups": 12,
 "shard_copies": 14,
 "restorable": true,
 "holders": [
 { "node_id": "…", "node_name": "pizza-1", "bytes": 1048576, "files": 21 },
 { "node_id": "…", "node_name": "pizza-2", "bytes": 1048576, "files": 21 }
 ]
 }
 ]
}

Request # 

GET /_cluster/trash

Response #

  • items — newest first; each item merges every node that still holds a copy of the data into holders.
  • kind — namespace or collection, parsed from the delete-time snapshot. Items without a snapshot (legacy items swept by the orphan scanner before snapshots existed, or a failed snapshot write) report restorable: false and cannot be restored.
  • retention_secs — the effective retention; items are physically deleted once older than this.
  • unreachable_nodes — members that could not be reached; the list may be incomplete for items they hold.

item.title: Delete a namespace
item.description:
Delete a namespace #

Delete an existing namespace.

Examples #

The following request delete the namespace called website:

DELETE /_namespace/website

Request # 

DELETE /_namespace/<name>

/_ns/<name> is accepted as a shorter alias.

Path parameters #

  • <name>
    (Required, string) The name of the namespace that you want to delete.

Response # 

{ "acknowledged": true }

Trash semantics #

Deleting a namespace moves the WHOLE namespace into the trash: every collection’s data directory is retained under <data_path>/trash/ together with a namespace-level restore snapshot (one snapshot per collection — schemas, shard UUIDs, partition routing, placements). The sweeper physically deletes it after trash.retention_secs.

item.title: Features
item.description:
Features #

Realtime #

  • True realtime search — a document is searchable the moment its write is acknowledged; there is no refresh and no near-real-time window. See How realtime works.
  • Write-ahead logging — local file WAL by default (Kafka-backed optional), with configurable durability (strict / batched / async) and crash-safe restart replay.

Updates #

  • Partial update — deep-merge doc bodies plus an ordered ops operator list (incr, append, rename, current_date, …), applied atomically under optimistic concurrency control.
  • In-place columns — "inplace": true numeric/boolean fields get O(1) column writes on a fast lane, independent checkpoints, and block-summary query pruning. See In-place columns.

Scaling #

  • Rolling-based sharding — collections partition into fixed-capacity rollings (4.2B docs each) that roll over automatically; infinite growth without reindexing. See Why named Pizza.
  • Online resharding — change a rolling’s shard count while every read and write keeps being served; documents keep their _id throughout, with a progress/status/events API.
  • Replication — Raft-replicated metadata, per-rolling replica counts, shard failover and re-allocation, and value-level replication of fast-lane inplace updates.

Search and analytics #

  • Full-text and term queries — match, match_phrase, query_string, bool, terms, exists, ranges, regexps, fuzzy, wildcard, spans, and more (see the search reference).
  • Geo, vector and relational queries — geo_bounding_box, geo_distance, vector (kNN) similarity, nested documents, join and graph traversal.
  • Semantic search — server-side text→vector inference through external OpenAI-compatible embedding services: vector fields mapped with source + model derive vectors at write time, queries accept plain text, and the semantic query needs no field knowledge at all. Hybrid search (BM25 + vector, RRF or linear fusion) ships natively and through the Elasticsearch retriever/knn forms; point-in-time reads pin consistent views for deep pagination.
  • Aggregations — metric, bucket and pipeline aggregations (see the aggregation reference).
  • Analysis — pluggable analyzers, per-collection custom analyzer definitions, and an analysis workbench API.
  • Elasticsearch syntax tolerance — common Elasticsearch request bodies are accepted as-is, easing migration.

Security #

  • API-key authentication with RBAC roles (platform_admin, operator, monitor, namespace_admin, read_write, read_only), Raft-replicated key minting/revocation, and a bootstrap-key flow. See Security.

Operations #

  • Runtime settings — region (cluster-wide, Raft-replicated) and node-level settings tunable without restart, including a dynamic log level; layered scope precedence with collection and rolling settings.
  • Manual maintenance — collection-wide and per-shard compaction, epoch roll/flush, batch flush tasks, all observable via node APIs.
  • Observability — cluster health/state, node recovery and build backlog, per-shard storage inspection, search slowlog and audit, and a built-in web console with a FIRE storage explorer. See Node observability.
  • CDC change feed — poll /_changes to replicate data to external systems. See Change feed (CDC).
  • Trash (recycle bin) — deleted data survives a retention window and can be restored.
  • Cluster admission — join tokens for controlled node admission, manual node removal, allocation dashboards. See Cluster management.

item.title: Indexing parameters
item.description:
Indexing parameters #

index #

For non-object fields, if set, Pizza would build an index for the field to make it searchable. For object fields, the index parameter overrides the index settings of its sub-fields.

Carried by: most scalar types and object — see each field type. Not carried by the vector types.

index_options #

Controls what information is added to the inverted index. Available options are:

  • docs: Only the doc number is indexed. Can answer the question Does this term exist in this field?
  • freqs: Doc number and term frequencies are indexed. Term frequencies are used to score repeated terms higher than single terms.
  • positions (default): Doc number, term frequencies, and term positions (or order) are indexed. Positions can be used for proximity or phrase queries.
  • offsets: Doc number, term frequencies, positions, and start and end character offsets (which map the term back to the original string) are indexed. Offsets are used by the unified highlighter to speed up highlighting.

Carried by: text, keyword.

item.title: Node Settings
item.description: Node settings are runtime-tunable knobs that apply to a single node. Every setting is a transient override over the persistent pizza.yml value (or the built-in default): a change takes effect immediately via PUT and disappears at restart — set the same key in the yml for a persistent value. This is the node-scope sibling of the Raft-replicated Region Settings: routing policy is cluster-wide, while log verbosity, search lane budgets and trash retention are per-node concerns.

item.title: Runtime node settings and dynamic log level
item.description:
Runtime node settings and dynamic log level #

Node-local knobs no longer require a restart. GET/PUT /_node/_local/settings exposes transient overrides over the pizza.yml values — search lane budgets, the slowlog threshold, the default search timeout, trash retention — and they take effect immediately:

# drop the slowlog threshold to 200ms on one node, effective immediately
curl -X PUT http://127.0.0.1:28000/_node/_local/settings \
 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
 -d '{"node.search.slow_threshold_ms": 200}'

The flagship: log.level flips live — no restart, no dropped requests — which turns “turn on debug logging on the suspicious node” into a one-liner while preserving target-specific directives like openraft=warn.

item.title: Verify a trash item
item.description:
Verify a trash item #

Run a read-only shard-completeness check on a trash item, across every node that still holds its data. Nothing is moved or written — this is the preflight for a restore.

Examples # 

POST /_cluster/trash/1788916375_namespace-website/verify

With ?deep=true, every present segment file additionally has its footer parsed — truncated or corrupted files are reported by name. Deep mode can take noticeably longer on large items.

{
 "item": "1788916375_namespace-website",
 "deep": false,
 "kind": "namespace",
 "namespace": "website",
 "restorable": true,
 "degraded": false,
 "shard_groups": [
 {
 "collection": "website:logs",
 "shard": "a1b2…",
 "expected_copies": 2,
 "complete_copies": 2,
 "copies": [
 { "node": "…", "node_name": "pizza-1", "primary": true, "complete": true },
 { "node": "…", "node_name": "pizza-2", "primary": false, "complete": true }
 ]
 }
 ],
 "issues": [],
 "unreachable_nodes": []
}

Request # 

POST /_cluster/trash/<item>/verify[?deep=true]

Path parameters #

  • <item>
    (Required, string) The trash item name, as listed by List the cluster trash.

Response #

  • restorable — true when every shard group with recorded data has at least one complete copy on some node. A shard group counts a copy as complete when its allocation directory AND its segment manifest with all declared local files are present (and, in deep mode, every file’s footer parses).
  • degraded — true when the item is restorable but some recorded copies are missing; the restore comes back with fewer replicas, which the allocator backfills.
  • issues — human-readable problem lines (missing directories, missing/corrupt segment files, unreachable nodes), each prefixed with the node it applies to.

item.title: Cluster management APIs
item.description:
Cluster management APIs #

Operator-facing /_cluster/* endpoints beyond health and state: the allocation dashboard, node removal, and join-token management.

Regions # 

GET /_cluster/_regions

A lightweight summary of every region this node knows about — identity (name, uuid, zone), leader, member nodes with their API/RPC addresses, and per-region counts. The region serving the request is marked local, telling you which /_cluster/_region/_local/... endpoints apply to it.

Allocation dashboard # 

GET /_cluster/allocation

The leader’s shard-allocation view: the effective cluster.routing.* settings, per-node shard load, the recent allocation/relocation task history (newest first) and how many tasks are in flight. Answers “what is the allocator doing right now”.

item.title: Collection-wide manual compaction
item.description:
Collection-wide manual compaction #

Reclaiming disk no longer means waiting for the background cadence or poking shards one by one. One request runs a merge pass on every started primary copy of the collection, cluster-wide:

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:28000/my-collection/_compact \
 -H 'Authorization: Bearer pz_bootstrap_key'

The response reports the queued batch job per hosting node — job id plus how many local primary passes it covers — so a node-level failure fails the row, not the request:

item.description:
Configuration file reference #

pizza.yml (the default lookup path, override with -c/--config <file>) is read once at startup. Unknown keys are rejected — the node refuses to start on a typo, and on a key that was renamed in an upgrade. Individual keys can be overridden per launch with pizza -E <key>=<value> (repeatable; values parse as YAML, e.g. -E node.network.binding=127.0.0.1:12200).

Secret values #

geo_point #

A latitude/longitude point ({"lat": 39.9, "lon": 116.4}), indexed for geo bounding box, geo distance and geo polygon queries. Distances use haversine on WGS-84 in metres.

item.title: Limitations
item.description:
Limitations #

Known limitations of the current release, and where to read more.

Storage and scaling #

  • 256 logical partitions per rolling are fixed — the partition count is a design constant, not a creation-time setting. What you scale is the number of physical shards (via the sharding strategy and online reshard).
  • Object storage and Parquet are optional, not the default — persistence is Pizza’s FIRE columnar format on local disk. S3-backed and Parquet-mount backends are opt-in engine features.

Cluster operations #

  • Cluster state is local-region only — GET /_cluster/state returns the serving region’s state; querying a remote region by UUID answers 501 not implemented yet (same for remote region health). The blocks and version state filters are accepted but are no-ops.
  • No backup/restore API yet — metadata is covered by Raft snapshots, but data backup is a manual data-directory procedure. See Backup and restore.
  • Collection-level replica changes apply to new rollings only — resizing the replicas of an existing rolling uses Update rolling settings; a rolling being resharded has its replica count frozen until the reshard commits.

Querying #

  • SQL/PRQL are subset-shaped — POST /_sql and POST /_prql serve a documented subset (see the SQL & PRQL reference): no JOIN across collections yet (planned), no subqueries, CTE (WITH), window functions or set operations; PRQL s-strings are rejected outright and pipelines that would lower into a CTE fail closed with a positioned error.
  • Scripting is aggregation- and search-scoped — scripts run in pipeline aggregations, scripted_metric, as the value source of the single-value metric aggs, in a search request’s script_fields, and in the scripted queries (script_score, script filters, _script sort; Rhai, sandboxed, see the scripts reference). A script filter applies to the collected window (aggregations are not narrowed); per-segment script filtering is not implemented.
  • CDC is poll-based — the change feed is a pull API bounded by WAL retention; a consumer that falls behind purged_below must run a full resync.

Security #

  • Tenancy is namespace-scoped 1:1 — a key’s tenant maps to a single namespace; there is no multi-namespace tenant grouping yet.

item.title: Architecture
item.description:
Architecture #

Pizza is a distributed search engine built on a shared-nothing design: every node owns its shards, memory, and disks — and within a node, every CPU core runs its own runtime instance, sharing nothing with the other cores. All disk and network I/O is asynchronous, running on a thread-per-core runtime ( monoio); on Linux, io_uring offloads the WAL’s durable-write fsyncs whenever the kernel supports it.

{ "deleted": true, "item": "1788916375_namespace-website", "nodes": 2 }

Request #

Variable Default Description

item.title: Realtime and in-place parameters
item.description:
Realtime and in-place parameters #

realtime #

For non-object fields, enabling this option allows the field to support real-time search. For object fields, the realtime parameter overrides the realtime settings of its sub-fields.

Carried by: every type — see each field type.

inplace #

For non-object numeric and boolean fields, enabling this option makes a dedicated column the authoritative store of the field’s value. Partial updates on such fields can be applied as O(1) in-place column writes instead of rebuilding the document, which keeps frequent counters and flags cheap — only some update operators qualify, and the whole request must target inplace fields; see fast-lane eligibility for the exact operator list and conditions. A partial update that mixes inplace fields with regular fields is supported as well, and the document keeps its _id either way. Values are visible the moment the write lands (search snapshots pin the document set, not the values); a missing numeric field starts from 0 and a missing boolean from false; integer arithmetic wraps on overflow. See In-place columns for the visibility, arithmetic, and query-pruning semantics.

item.title: Vector types
item.description:
Vector types #

semantic_text #

The field type for semantic search: declare one field, writes embed it server-side, and the semantic query searches it with plain text — no field names, no manual vectors.

PUT /my-collection
{
 "schema": {
 "properties": {
 "body": {
 "type": "semantic_text",
 "service": "zai",
 "model": "GLM-4.6V",
 "dims": 3072,
 "similarity": "cosine"
 }
 }
 }
}

Documents carry plain text ({"body": "some text"}); the vector derives at write time into the internal body.embedding sub-field. The field is pure semantic: the text is kept in _source but is not inverted-indexed — match/term queries do not hit it; search goes through the derived vectors. A sibling regular text field plus bool.should composition gives hybrid retrieval.

item.title: AI Services
item.description: AI services are the external, OpenAI-compatible model endpoints behind server-side inference — schema-driven text→vector derivation, text vector queries, the semantic query and the /_embedding API on the embedding side, and the POST /_chat generation facade on the other. Every service speaks the OpenAI wire format: the embeddings API (POST {url} with {"model", "input": [...]} and a bearer key), and — once it lists generation models — the chat-completions API at its chat_url.

item.title: Compact a collection
item.description:
Compact a collection #

Queue one manual compaction (merge) pass on every started primary copy of the collection, cluster-wide. Useful when you want to reclaim disk space or reduce the segment count on demand, without waiting for the background compaction cadence.

The API is asynchronous: it fans out to at most one request per node hosting a started primary, and each node queues its own batch compaction job (one job per node, mutual exclusion — HTTP 409 from that node’s row while one runs). The request returns as soon as the jobs are queued; a pass can run for minutes, so nothing waits for the merges. Per-shard job state and live merge progress (phase, per-mille) are observable in each node’s task view, and a job is cancellable there too. A node-level failure fails that node’s row, not the whole request.

item.title: Empty the trash everywhere
item.description:
Empty the trash everywhere #

Physically delete every trashed item on every node, without waiting for the retention window. This cannot be undone.

Examples # 

POST /_cluster/trash/empty

{ "nodes": 2, "removed": 5 }

Request # 

POST /_cluster/trash/empty

item.title: Flush a collection
item.description:
Flush a collection #

Queue a flush of every live shard copy of the collection, cluster-wide — primaries and started replicas. A flush seals the shard’s mutable state into the WAL and builds a new immutable .fire segment from the WAL tail, turning in-memory writes into durable segment storage so the WAL can be purged afterwards.

Both a flush and a Compact a collection request queue node-local jobs that run asynchronously — the request returns as soon as the jobs are queued. Track or cancel them on the node’s task list (GET /_node/_local/tasks): flush jobs under flush_jobs, compaction under compaction_tasks[]. Only one flush job runs per node at a time — a node already running one answers 409 in its row. The difference is what the job does: compaction merges existing immutable segments, a flush seals the mutable tail into a new one.

item.title: Object and nested types
item.description:
Object and nested types #

object #

JSON documents are hierarchical in nature: the document may contain inner objects which, in turn, may contain inner objects themselves. The object type introduces inner objects.

{

 "artists": ["Bill Danoff", "Taffy Nivert", "John Denver"]
 }
}

  • index — an object field’s index parameter would overwrite its sub-fields’ index parameter, even when they are explicitly set.
  • properties
  • profile
  • source / column / store

item.title: Why named Pizza
item.description:
Why named Pizza? #

Do you wonder why this project is named Pizza?

To infinity scaling #

Pizza solves the challenge of managing massive data seamlessly. Imagine creating a collection and continuously adding documents, from zero to petabytes, without the need to worry about sharding or reindexing. Scaling your machine becomes effortless, ensuring a smooth, seamless, and painless experience for application developers.

Sharding puzzle #

One of the world’s three major challenges: What is the appropriate size for an index shard?

item.title: How realtime works
item.description:
How realtime works? #

Do you like to let your customer wait? #

[Pizza in Realtime]

A document written to Pizza is searchable the moment its write is acknowledged — there is no refresh, no near-real-time window, and nothing to tune to get there. This page walks the write path that makes that true.

The write path #

  1. WAL first. The write is appended to the shard’s write-ahead log (a local file-based WAL by default; a Kafka-backed WAL is available). Durability follows wal.local.durability — strict fsyncs per append, batched (the default) group-commits by size and timeout, async skips the hot-path fsync entirely.
  2. Mutable layer. The live documents are indexed into the shard’s in-memory mutable layer, which is itself searchable — this is what removes the refresh: reads see the mutable layer and the immutable segments in one snapshot, so the visibility point is the write’s acknowledgement.
  3. Epoch freeze and build. When the active epoch crosses a size or ops threshold (wal.local.epoch_freeze_max_bytes / epoch_freeze_max_ops, runtime-tunable), it is frozen and built in the background into an immutable FIRE segment. The build does not gate reads or writes.
  4. WAL purge. Once a segment is durably built (per wal.local.segment_durability), the WAL entries it supersedes are purged, bounded by the retention window (wal.local.retention_epoch / retention_bytes).

Recovery is the mirror image: on restart, a shard replays its WAL tail over its last durable segments, so acknowledged writes survive crashes. Restart replay and peer recovery are both bounded by node.recovery_concurrency.

item.title: Keystore
item.description:
Keystore #

The keystore is a node-local file of secrets referenced from pizza.yml — API keys and tokens never have to live in the config file itself. Entries resolve through ${keystore:NAME} references:

node:
 embedding:
 endpoints:
 - name: openai
 url: https://api.openai.com/v1/embeddings
 api_key: ${keystore:openai}

The file is <config dir>/keystore.json — next to the config file it serves, so one instance per config (multi-instance hosts keep separate keystores) and it never enters the data directory’s lifecycle. It is written 0600 and replaced atomically; entries never enter cluster metadata, raft logs, or API responses — views answer with a masked hint only (sk-…4f2a).

item.title: Keystore hot-reload
item.description:
Keystore hot-reload #

Rotating a secret no longer restarts the node. ${keystore:...} references re-resolve into the running configuration on demand: console edits trigger the reload themselves, and out-of-band changes (a CLI edit, a replaced mounted Secret) are one call away.

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:28000/_node/_local/keystore/_reload \
 -H 'Authorization: Bearer pz_bootstrap_key'

The answer says exactly what happened — key names only, values stay write-only:

{
 "entries": 3,
 "read_only": false,
 "references": 2,
 "changed": ["node.embedding.endpoints", "catalog.join_token"],
 "unchanged": 0,
 "failed": []
}

A rotated embedding API key applies to the next inference call; a rotated catalog.join_token to the next join attempt. A reference whose entry disappeared keeps its running value and lands in failed until the entry returns — reload never aborts the node the way a missing entry aborts boot.

item.title: Relation type
item.description:
Relation type #

relation #

A graph edge value ({"from": ..., "to": ...}, by document id or key) that materializes adjacency for the traverse query and the graph projection block. The relation parameter declares the connected types.

Parameters for relation fields #

  • realtime
  • index
  • relation (from_type / to_type meta)

Support indexing multiple values #

Yes — a document may carry multiple edges.

item.title: Roll over a collection
item.description:
Roll over a collection #

Allocate a new rolling for the collection now, regardless of whether the active rolling is full — subsequent writes go to the new rolling. This is the manual form of the automatic rollover that happens when a rolling reaches its document capacity.

The change is replicated through Raft (the same metadata request used by automatic rollovers), so the shard groups of the new rolling are created on every node.

item.title: Type-specific parameters
item.description:
Type-specific parameters #

Parameters bound to a single type family.

format #

For date fields, the accepted input format(s) — default strict_date_optional_time||epoch_millis; multiple formats join with ||.

Carried by: date.

vector_options #

For vector fields — dims, similarity, index_type (flat, HNSW, BBQ or TurboQuant variants), plus tuning knobs (m, ef_construction, ef_search) and, for declarative semantic embedding, model, source and service (the AI-service disambiguator when several services list the same model id). The full catalog lives on the vector search page; the semantic_text type is the sugar form over the same wiring.

item.title: Model features & the /_chat facade
item.description:
Model features & the /_chat facade #

Every model in the AI-services registry can now declare what it is for and what it accepts — features (embedding or generation) and inputs (text or image). The two axes are orthogonal: “multimodal” is not a category of its own but an inputs list beyond text.

node:

 url: https://api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4/embeddings

 api_key: sk-…

 - embedding-3  # embedding + text (the defaults)
 - {id: GLM-4.6V, dims: 3072} # embedding, dims declared
 - {id: glm-4-flash, features: [generation]}  # text generation

Omitted fields keep the historical defaults, so every existing plain-string listing still means embedding + text — nothing to migrate.

item.title: Relational parameters
item.description:
Relational parameters #

The cross-type parameters that turn a flat schema into a relational one: declare a foreign key, opt into reference materialization, and route placement by the field’s value. They compose — the same org_id field can declare all four — and the joins tutorial walks them end to end against a live node.

references #

Declares this field as a foreign key into another collection. The value is the referenced collection’s document key (or, with a field-targeted join, whatever field the join names).

item.description:
Cluster-wide recycle bin #

Accidental deletes used to be a race against the sweeper: deleting a namespace only dropped metadata, and the data directories drifted into the trash WITHOUT a recovery snapshot — permanently unrestorable. The recycle bin is now a first-class, cluster-wide surface with a namespace-centric view, a pre-restore integrity check, and one-request restore:

GET /_cluster/trash

item.title: How query works
item.description:
How query works? #

A search request fans out from the coordinating node to every shard copy of the target collections, executes against a snapshot of the index, and merges ranked results back — this page walks that pipeline and the mechanisms that keep it fast:

graph LR R["search request"] --> C("coordinator") C -->|"one copy per shard group —
saturated nodes are skipped"| G0("shard group 0 — any copy") C --> G1("shard group 1 — any copy") C --> G2("shard group 2 — any copy") G0 --> Q["top-K + aggs against the snapshot —
mutable layer + immutable segments"] G1 --> Q G2 --> Q Q --> M("merge — rank, dedupe, paginate") M --> H["hits and aggregations,
or partial results on timeout"]

item.title: Host & capability probes — see the machine, not just the node
item.description:
Host & capability probes — see the machine, not just the node #

Every node now reports what its host actually is and what it can actually do, on GET /_node/_local under host: the OS distribution and kernel, NUMA topology (node count + per-node CPU lists and distances), NIC inventory with negotiated link speeds, the data disk’s bus (NVMe or not) with its I/O scheduler and atime policy, the container and seccomp environment, the DMI platform, transparent-hugepage state — and the resource ceilings: fd limit vs usage, mmap count vs max_map_count, swap, conntrack fill, TCP sysctls, and cgroup CPU/memory quotas with throttle counts. The stats API adds a steal_percent trend — the noisy-neighbor line on shared tenancy.

item.title: Lesson 1 — First search
item.description:
Lesson 1 — First search #

Start the node, index documents, run your first queries, and watch them update in real time.

The use case #

Your application produces a stream of documents — logs, events, messages — and they are only useful if they are searchable the moment they land: no nightly batch, no refresh call, no second system to keep in sync. The questions this lesson answers:

item.title: Use cases
item.description:
Use cases #

Pizza is built for latency-sensitive search over fresh, mutable data at scale. The scenarios below map to concrete features — follow the links for the mechanics.

Operational logs and events, searchable the moment they land #

Observability and security pipelines need indexed events and fresh results — “what happened in the last minute” cannot wait for a refresh window. Pizza’s realtime write path makes every acknowledged write searchable immediately, rollings absorb unbounded growth without reindexing, and high-volume ingest is served by batched WAL writes plus background segment builds that never gate reads.

item.title: Analyze text
item.description:
Analyze text #

The analysis workbench: run the server’s tokenizers, normalizers, token filters and analyzers over sample text and see the exact token stream — the same components the indexing path uses, so what you debug here is exactly what collections run. The analysis chain decides what is searchable: query and document must reduce to the same tokens.

How it works #

Every analyzer is assembled from three stages, run in this order:

item.title: Avg aggregation
item.description:
Avg aggregation #

A single-value metrics aggregation that computes the average of numeric values that are extracted from the aggregated documents. It summarizes “what does a typical matching document look like on this field” into one number — the question SQL spells AVG(price) — without fetching a single document.

How it works #

The engine walks the matching documents once, keeping a running sum and count; the result is sum / count. Nothing is estimated: the average is exact. Values are coerced to doubles as they are read — integers, floats and booleans (true = 1, false = 0) contribute, non-numeric values such as keyword strings do not.

item.title: Avg bucket aggregation
item.description:
Avg bucket aggregation #

A sibling pipeline aggregation computing the average of a metric across another aggregation’s buckets. Bucket aggregations answer “what is the revenue per day / per category / per range”; avg_bucket rolls those per-bucket numbers into one mean — “what does a typical day or category bring in” — without a second query or client-side arithmetic.

"avg_day": { "avg_bucket": { "buckets_path": "per_day>revenue" } }

How it works #

avg_bucket is declared next to the bucket aggregation it consumes (a sibling in the same aggs object) and runs after every regular aggregation has finished — after the merge, too, in a distributed search. It reads the parent’s finished buckets, collects one number per bucket, and divides their sum by their count. The result is a single-value metric ({"value": 56.25}) placed alongside the parent.

item.title: Distance feature
item.description:
Distance feature query #

Recalls every document and scores each by its proximity to an origin — the closer, the higher:

score = boost × pivot / (pivot + distance(document, origin))

A document exactly at the origin scores boost; one pivot units away scores boost / 2. The decay is gradual — unlike a range filter, a document three pivots out still scores boost / 4, so nothing is excluded, only demoted. It answers “rank by recency or by distance” without a second index or a script.

item.title: Geo-bounding-box query
item.description:
Geo-bounding-box query #

Matches documents whose geo_point field falls inside a rectangle defined by its top-left and bottom-right corners. Coordinates are WGS-84 degrees; filtering only (does not contribute distance scoring).

It is the cheapest geographic filter. When the region you need is a rectangle of latitude and longitude — a map viewport, a city’s extents, a country’s outline approximated by its bounds — the engine answers with a single index range and no per-document geometry math.

item.title: Lesson 2 — Text search
item.description:
Lesson 2 — Text search #

How text actually matches: analysis, exact terms, phrases, and the error-tolerant family. Everything below runs live on the logs collection (150 documents with message, level, host, url.path).

The use case #

The search box in front of users — application logs, product descriptions, support tickets. Users type in one casing, with typos, and your data is cased differently; the craft is choosing the right amount of looseness per question:

item.title: Match query
item.description:
Match query #

Returns documents that match a provided text, number, date or boolean value. The provided text is analyzed before matching — this is the primary full-text query.

Inside a nested query: supported — the text is matched per array element.

How it works #

The engine resolves the analyzer first — the analyzer parameter when given, else the field’s search analyzer, else the built-in standard analyzer — and runs it over the query text. Each resulting token becomes one term clause:

item.title: Nested query
item.description:
Nested query #

Matches parent documents whose nested sub-documents — objects mapped with "nested": true — satisfy a query within one element at a time. It exists because a flattened object index cannot keep two field values inside the same array element together — the pitfall the next section makes concrete.

The cross-element problem #

A flattened index correlates across array elements, not within them: variants.color = blue AND variants.size = L matches a document as soon as some element is blue and some element is L — not necessarily the same one. The teaching dataset’s products makes the difference visible (each element pairs blue with L, never with M):

item.title: PRQL queries
item.description:
PRQL queries #

POST /_prql accepts PRQL pipeline text in the same request shape as POST /_sql — query, plus cursor, params, snapshot_id and timeout riding alongside exactly as they do for SQL. The statement is compiled by a pinned prqlc and executed as its equivalent SQL through the identical pipeline, so cursors, snapshots, timeouts and the response envelope behave the same (see SQL & PRQL).

A cursor walk resubmits the SAME PRQL text plus the cursor object; the compiled statement is cached by text, so the walk compiles once.

item.title: Relations that route — joins, FK placement, salting
item.description:
Relations that route — joins, FK placement, salting #

A fact collection can now behave like one. Declare the relationship in the schema and the engine takes over:

"org_id": {
 "type": "keyword",
 "immutable": true,
 "references": {"collection": "orgs"},
 "routing": true,
 "ref": true
}
  • Join queries are live — a semi-join over the wire: the inner query runs on the referenced collection, its matching keys become a membership filter on the outer side, and joins through a declared references field resolve without a second fan-out.
  • Writes place by the foreign key’s value — hash(org_id) picks the home partition, not the document key, so an org’s facts colocate. Key-addressed operations take ?routing=<value> ( fetch, update, delete).
  • Salting splits the hot org — when one routing value dominates, the _salting API spreads its writes across a partition SET (deterministic per key, round-robin for auto-IDs), with a terms feed that flags candidates against your threshold. Assignments are never auto-applied and searches stay oblivious — salting changes placement, never visibility.

One declaration, three consequences:

item.title: Roadmap
item.description:
Roadmap #

A living list of what is planned next. Items land when they are done — the limitations page tracks the counterpart “what does not work today”.

Querying and analytics #

  • SQL — the query subset over the search DSL is live on POST /_sql — filter/aggregate/sort/paginate, $1 parameters, PIT snapshots, grouped cursor pages — with POST /_prql alongside it (see the SQL & PRQL reference and the syntax walkthrough). The frontend now lives in the engine (feature sql), and the WebAssembly build runs statements through the same parse/lower (search_with_sql) — the base for SQL demos in the live playground. What remains: JOIN across collections, subqueries, window functions, the EXPLAIN lowering trace, the two-layer cache closeout, and the playground rollout (envelope parity plus demo pages).

Storage #

  • Object storage backends — the segment file layout is already object-storage-friendly (content-addressed write-once files, generationed manifests with replication-safe publish ordering, so an external replicator can mirror a shard to S3/OSS). What remains is the first-class option: storage-tier configuration, bucket lifecycle and recovery straight from remote storage.
  • Parquet interop — the engine already reads Parquet columns through its column API (opt-in engine feature). What remains is the user-facing mount: exposing standard Parquet data as a collection, as an exchange format with big-data systems.

Operations #

  • Backup and restore API — point-in-time snapshots with restore semantics, replacing today’s manual data-directory procedure (see Backup and restore).
  • Cluster-wide state and health — aggregating /_cluster/state and health across regions instead of the serving region only.

AI and semantic search #

  • Chunking for semantic_text — long-document semantic search: split field text into overlapping chunks, embed each, keep several vectors per document, score by the best-matching chunk. Blocked on engine support for multiple vectors per (document, field) — today’s vector store keeps exactly one (FlatVectorStore::add overwrites), so this spans the mutable store, the epoch builder, the HNSW index and score aggregation. Until then the field embeds whole texts in one call (fine for titles, names, log lines; bounded by the model’s input limit), and long documents have a working pattern: chunk into child documents at write time, search with the semantic query and collapse by parent id (see field collapsing).

Multi-tenancy #

  • Tenant grouping — namespaces grouped under one tenant identity, generalizing today’s 1:1 namespace mapping.

item.title: Sort and pagination
item.description:
Sort and pagination #

Control which documents come back and in what order — sort, from/size, search_after/search_before, and total-hit accounting.

POST /my-collection/_search

How it works #

sort is an array of sort clauses evaluated in order; the first clause that produces a difference decides the order. Sorting on an indexed field lets the collector skip documents that cannot make the cut (early termination), so field sorts — and _doc above all — are cheaper than score sorts, not just differently ordered.

item.title: Term query
item.description:
Term query #

Returns documents that contain an exact term in a provided field.

You can use the term query to find documents based on a precise value such as a price, a product ID, or a username. It is also the atom the rest of the term-level family resolves to: terms expands into a should of term clauses, and prefix / wildcard / regexp / fuzzy all resolve to term sets before execution.

item.title: Terms aggregation
item.description:
Terms aggregation #

A multi-bucket value source based aggregation where buckets are dynamically built - one per unique value. It answers “group by this field, count (and aggregate) per value” without knowing the values in advance, which a fixed-bucket aggregation like histogram or range cannot do.

How it works #

Every matching document is placed in the bucket keyed by its value of field. Multi-valued fields bucket per element: a document whose tags holds ["search", "architecture"] is counted once in the search bucket and once in the architecture bucket. Documents without the field are skipped — unless missing is set, in which case they land together in one bucket keyed by that value.

item.title: Vector query (kNN)
item.description:
Vector query (kNN) #

Finds the k nearest neighbors of a query vector — similarity search over dense_vector / sparse_vector fields. The query vector can be supplied directly, or as natural-language text that the serving layer embeds with the field’s configured model (schema-driven semantic search).

How it works #

Execution depends on where the documents live:

  • Realtime (not yet flushed) — an exact brute-force scan over the mutable store: every vector is scored, a size-k min-heap keeps the best, and a filter (see below) is tested before any distance is computed.
  • Flushed segments — the field’s index_type decides: flat scans the stored f32 vectors (exact, O(N·dims)); the graph types (hnsw_flat, turbo_quant_hnsw, bbq_hnsw) traverse the persisted HNSW graph with distances computed on the flat vectors — scores stay exact and only an ef-bounded neighborhood is evaluated; the quantized scans (turbo_quant, bbq_flat) score compact codes for a k × oversampling candidate pool and rescore it with full precision (approximate). The per-type breakdown is in Index types.

Scores follow the field’s similarity (overridable per query, but it must match the schema): cosine is the cosine similarity in [-1.0, 1.0]; dot_product the raw dot product; l2 scores as the negated squared Euclidean distance — 0 means identical vectors. Higher is always more similar, so one top-k heap serves all three.

item.title: Built-in analysis components
item.description:
Built-in analysis components #

The server ships 83 analyzers, 50 tokenizers, 15 normalizers and 327 token filters, registered at startup. The authoritative, always-current list on YOUR node is:

GET /_analysis/components

Components are referenced by name — in a field’s schema ("analyzer": "english"), in a custom analyzer definition, or in an ad-hoc _analysis/analyze pipeline.

How it works #

The catalog is assembled in two layers. The engine core registers the minimal set that is always present: the standard and whitespace tokenizers, the lowercase normalizer, the lowercase/uppercase/ stopwords token filters, and the two named analyzers composed from them (standard, whitespace). Every other name below comes from the ~40 analysis plugin crates under contrib/analysis-*, registered at startup in one pass — foundation plugins first (core, stemmers, icu), then the CJK and per-language plugins, which intentionally override the basic analyzers from core with richer pipelines (language stop words, normalization, stemming).

item.title: Cardinality aggregation
item.description:
Cardinality aggregation #

A single-value metrics aggregation that counts the number of distinct values of a field — how many different types were sold, how many different hosts logged, how many different authors wrote.

How it works #

The engine counts with a HyperLogLog++ sketch — tuned so that small counts stay exact:

  • Values are hashed (MurmurHash3, 64-bit) into a sketch that keeps an exact set while the number of distinct values stays at or below precision_threshold; those counts are returned verbatim.
  • Above the threshold the sketch promotes to dense HyperLogLog registers, so memory stops growing with the data: roughly 1.6% relative error at the default threshold of 3000, tightening to about 0.4% at the maximum of 40000. The returned value is always a rounded whole number.
  • When documents lack the field and missing is set, they all count as one additional distinct value; without missing they are simply not counted.

Distributed queries ship the sketch itself with each shard’s partial result and the coordinating node unions the sketches before estimating — the same number a single-node execution over all shards' documents would produce. (Cardinality nested inside bucket sub-aggregations still merges its per-shard finalized counts by maximum, a lower bound, when no sketch travels with them.)

item.title: Geo-distance query
item.description:
Geo-distance query #

Matches documents whose geo_point field lies within a great-circle distance of a centre point. Distances are in metres.

This is the “find me things nearby” query: given one centre and one radius, it returns exactly the documents inside that disc on the sphere — the shape behind store locators, delivery zones and proximity alerts.

How it works #

The field is the same two-dimensional (lat, lon) BKD tree the other geo queries use (points indexed in any of the three ingest forms — object, [lon, lat] array, "lat,lon" string). Execution is two-phase:

item.title: Highlighting
item.description:
Highlighting #

Ask for matched fragments of your text fields back alongside each hit, with the matched terms wrapped in tags — ready to render as a search result list.

POST /my-collection/_search

How it works #

Highlighting is an engine-native enrich step that runs on the returned page only — after ranking and truncation, exactly like script fields. It has two phases (lib/engine/src/search/highlight/):

1. Term extraction. The engine walks the query tree and collects (field, term) pairs worth highlighting: term, terms, fuzzy, span_term, intervals, match, multi_match, match_phrase, and bool clauses. Text queries (match, multi_match, phrase) are re-tokenized through the field’s search analyzer (or the query’s explicit analyzer override), so the highlighted terms mirror what the query scored. must_not clauses never contribute — documents excluded by them get no tags from them. match_all, range, geo and vector queries carry nothing to highlight.

item.title: Intervals and more-like-this queries
item.description:
Intervals and more-like-this queries #

Two Elasticsearch-compatible queries landed natively in the engine — no more shape-shifting through match_phrase compositions.

intervals is a rule language over term positions. Say “these two phrases within two positions of each other, but only if neither overlaps this third one”:

POST /my-collection/_search
{
 "query": {
 "intervals": {
 "body": {
 "all_of": {
 "ordered": true,
 "intervals": [
 { "match": { "query": "search engine", "max_gaps": 0, "ordered": true } },
 { "match": { "query": "ranking", "max_gaps": 2 } }
 ],
 "filter": { "not_overlapping": { "match": { "query": "deprecated" } } }
 }
 }
 }
 }
}

Eight rule shapes (match, all_of, any_of, prefix, wildcard, fuzzy, regexp, range) and eight positional filter predicates (containing, before, not_overlapping, …) compose into one tree. Unsupported knobs are rejected with named errors instead of silently ignored — ask for a script filter and you will be told no.

item.title: Join query
item.description:
Join query #

Status: functional (semi-join). Joins need a running node — the gateway orchestrates and the engine executes, which is why the wasm playground does not host them. The joins tutorial walks the complete relational sequence — references → join → FK-routed writes → salting → ?routing= addressing — step by step against a live node.

Matches documents in the outer collection — the one in the request URL — whose field values intersect the join_on values of documents matching a query on the inner collection — the one named by target. The result is a semi-join: outer documents that have at least one matching inner document, each reported once. It is the moral equivalent of SQL’s

item.title: Lesson 3 — Structure and numbers
item.description:
Lesson 3 — Structure and numbers #

Ranges, sorts, and cursor pagination over the sales collection (120 documents: type, price, qty, amount, merchant, status, date).

The use case #

Most queries are not about words — they are filters and ordering over the structured half of the document: prices, quantities, timestamps. And real interfaces page through result sets, sometimes deeply. The questions this lesson answers:

  • “Sales priced $45 to $60” / “everything from 2024” — range over a typed field.
  • “Top 5 by amount” — the canonical sort clause.
  • “Page 3000 of a big result set, without re-ranking the world” — cursor pagination (search_after), where from+size breaks down.
  • “Why did my filter miss the row with 45?” — the field-type system: 45 the number and "45" the keyword are different values.

The types behind the data #

Numbers are indexed as their real types (float for price, integers for qty), dates as epoch millis. That is what makes the queries below precise — see the field types reference for the full catalog.

item.title: Multi terms aggregation
item.description:
Multi terms aggregation #

A multi-bucket aggregation like terms, but the bucket key is a TUPLE of values from several fields — e.g. every (merchant, status) combination. It answers cross-tab questions — “rows by column” tables — that a single-field terms aggregation cannot express without chaining requests.

How it works #

Each entry in the terms array contributes one component of the composite key. A document is placed in the bucket keyed by the tuple of its values, and the response reports each bucket’s key as an array — ["infini-store", "pending"].

item.title: Multi-vector query
item.description:
Multi-vector query #

Executes several vector queries — each targeting a (potentially different) vector field — and fuses their results into one ranking.

One document often has more than one useful representation: a title embedding and a body embedding, a dense vector and a learned-sparse vector, an image embedding beside its caption. A single vector query can read only one of them; this query runs them all and merges the rankings.

item.title: Phrase query
item.description:
Phrase query #

Returns documents that contain the exact sequence of terms, in order, with no other terms in between (modulo slop). The text is analyzed before matching, like the match query.

The query’s native name is phrase; the match_phrase spelling deserializes to the same query — an accepted alias, not a different feature.

Inside a nested query: supported — the phrase, including its slop, must be satisfied by ONE array element; terms keep query order.

item.title: Sum bucket aggregation
item.description:
Sum bucket aggregation #

A sibling pipeline aggregation computing the sum of a metric across another aggregation’s buckets — e.g. “total of the daily totals”. Where avg_bucket characterizes the typical bucket, sum_bucket re-totals the per-bucket values, which is how you grand-total a figure that was only computed per group.

"grand_total": { "sum_bucket": { "buckets_path": "per_day>revenue" } }

How it works #

sum_bucket is declared next to the bucket aggregation it consumes and runs after every regular aggregation — including the distributed merge — has finished. It walks the parent’s finished buckets, collects one number per bucket, and adds them up into a single-value metric ({"value": 6750}) placed alongside the parent.

item.title: Terms query
item.description:
Terms query #

Returns documents that contain one or more exact terms in a provided field. Equivalent to a boolean should of individual term queries — a document matches if it contains any of the values.

Inside a nested query: not supported yet — the clause is rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause. Expand into a bool should of term clauses instead.

How it works #

The planner expands the query before execution: each value becomes a term clause inside a BooleanQuery with minimum_should_match: 1, and a single-value terms collapses straight into one bare term query. Everything said on the term page about verbatim lookup, index routing (dictionary for keyword/text, BKD for numeric/date, Bool column for boolean) and BM25 scoring therefore applies per value here, with the per-value scores OR-ed together.

item.title: Credits
item.description:
Credits #

Pizza stands on the shoulders of the Rust and information-retrieval communities. This page credits the software we build on — and the projects whose ideas we learn from.

Reference points #

  • Lucene — decades of query semantics and scoring design that the DSL and scoring model learn from.
  • Elasticsearch — the JSON query DSL and REST API surface (_search, _doc, _bulk) the gateway is modeled on.
  • tantivy — the Rust search library our inverted-index benchmarks measure against, on the corpus and golden queries of the search-benchmark-game. No tantivy code runs inside Pizza — the engine is written from scratch, a different engine end to end, built to go far beyond it.

Engine core #

The search engine (lib/engine) is a no_std-capable crate that compiles from server to browser; these crates make that possible:

item.title: Geo-polygon query
item.description:
Geo-polygon query #

Matches documents whose geo_point field lies inside an arbitrary polygon. The ring is given as points in (lat, lon) order; vertices on the boundary count as inside, and holes can be modelled with a concave ring.

Real regions are rarely rectangular. City limits, districts, service areas and lakes have corners everywhere — this query filters points by an exact ring instead of the four edges of a bounding box.

item.title: Hybrid search and scoring pipeline
item.description:
Hybrid search and scoring pipeline #

Pizza runs lexical (BM25) and vector retrieval side by side and gives you explicit, composable stages to combine and re-shape scores:

graph LR B("bm25 leg") --> F("fuse
rrf / linear / disjmax") V("vector leg") --> F F --> SC("score_functions
per-document function scoring") P["a plain query,
no retrieve"] --> SC SC --> RS("rescore
second pass on the top window") RS --> H["one ranked list"]

Every stage is optional and combines with a plain query: use score_functions alone on a keyword search, or the full chain for hybrid retrieval.

item.title: Keys query
item.description:
Keys query #

Returns documents whose key is in the provided set. There is no field argument — the match is against the document identity itself, and values that do not exist in the collection are skipped.

The query’s native name is keys: it speaks Pizza’s _key vocabulary, the same word the REST API uses for by-key addressing. The ids spelling deserializes to the same query — an accepted alias, not a different feature.

item.title: Lesson 4 — Aggregations
item.description:
Lesson 4 — Aggregations #

From counts to histograms to composite paging — over sales and logs, with known answers you can verify by hand.

The use case #

Dashboards, reports, and faceted navigation — wherever the deliverable is not a page of hits but an answer. The questions this lesson answers:

  • “What is the average / min / max price?” — metric aggregations.
  • “How is revenue split by status?” — terms buckets.
  • “Volume per week / per price band” — histograms.
  • “Every (merchant, day) pair, complete — not just the top N” — composite aggregations with after cursors.
  • “Just the number, skip the hits” — size: 0.

Metric aggregations #

One number out: sum, avg, min, max, stats (all of them at once), cardinality (distinct values):

item.title: Max aggregation
item.description:
Max aggregation #

A single-value metrics aggregation that keeps track and returns the maximum value among the numeric values extracted from the aggregated documents. It answers “how high does this field go” over any query — the top of a price range, the latest timestamp in a window, the biggest order that matches a filter.

How it works #

The engine walks the matching documents once, keeping the largest value seen; any smaller value costs one comparison. Values are coerced to doubles as they are read — integers, floats and booleans (true = 1, false = 0) qualify, non-numeric values such as keyword strings do not.

item.title: Min bucket aggregation
item.description:
Min bucket aggregation #

A sibling pipeline aggregation identifying the smallest per-bucket metric value. Bucket aggregations rank groups by their own key or doc_count; min_bucket answers the orthogonal question — which of the per-bucket numbers (a revenue, a latency, a rate) is the lowest, and how low.

"worst_seller": { "min_bucket": { "buckets_path": "per_type>revenue" } }

How it works #

min_bucket is declared next to the bucket aggregation it consumes and runs after every regular aggregation — including the distributed merge — has finished. It walks the parent’s finished buckets, collects one number per bucket, and returns their minimum as a single-value metric ({"value": 1350}) placed alongside the parent. Only the value is returned — not which bucket produced it; read the parent’s bucket list when you need the winner’s key.

item.title: Multi-match query
item.description:
Multi-match query #

Returns documents that match a provided text across several fields — like the match query, with per-field boosts and multi-field scoring strategies.

Inside a nested query: supported — fields under the nested path are matched per array element.

How it works #

multi_match is expanded before execution (Query::simplify) into a tree the segment executors already know:

  1. Each entry in fields — after splitting off a ^boost suffix — becomes one match query over that field, carrying the query-level boost multiplied by the field boost ("title^3" → per-field boost 3).
  2. For type: "phrase" and type: "phrase_prefix" each field instead becomes a phrase query with slop: 0. The prefix part is not implemented: phrase_prefix currently behaves as an exact phrase and does not expand its last term as a prefix.
  3. Two or more fields are wrapped in a bool whose should clauses are the per-field queries, with at least one field required; a single field collapses to that field’s query — a plain match.

Scores: should clauses add their per-document scores (the bool default). The type additionally picks the combination used when one field name resolves to several indexed sub-fields — best_fields keeps the maximum, most_fields and cross_fields sum. cross_fields does not blend term statistics across fields; each field scores independently and the results merge.

item.title: Prefix query
item.description:
Prefix query #

Returns documents that contain a specific prefix in a provided field.

Use it when the values share a known beginning — a hostname family, an ID scheme, a URL section — and you want every term that starts with it.

Inside a nested query: not supported yet — the clause is rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause.

How it works #

The prefix is expanded against the inverted index’s term dictionary. Because the dictionary is kept in sorted order, the expansion is an ordered seek to the first term greater than or equal to the prefix, followed by reading the subtree of terms that start with it — no scan of the whole dictionary. Each expanded term’s postings are then unioned (OR semantics), exactly as if you had written a should of term queries.

item.title: Rare terms aggregation
item.description:
Rare terms aggregation #

A multi-bucket aggregation that keeps only RARE terms — bucket keys whose document count is at or below max_doc_count. The mirror image of terms for finding the long tail: instead of the top-N most frequent values, it returns every low-frequency value.

How it works #

Bucketing works exactly like terms: one bucket per unique value of field, multi-valued fields counted per element, and documents without the field either skipped or folded into a missing bucket. include/exclude filter candidate keys up front (exact-value arrays or a single wildcard string prefix* / *suffix).

item.title: Sandboxed scripting — scripted_metric, script_fields, script_score
item.description:
Sandboxed scripting — scripted_metric, script_fields, script_score #

Scripts landed across the whole request path — the engine runs the examples from the Elasticsearch docs unmodified. The engine is Rhai rather than Painless, but doc['x'].value, _score and params.<name> mean what they mean there.

Aggregations. scripted_metric runs your own four-phase map/reduce — init_script, map_script, combine_script, reduce_script — with per-segment states folded at the end. The single-value metric aggs (sum, avg, min, max, cardinality) accept a script in place of a field ( details), and pipeline aggregations keep their buckets_path arithmetic.

item.title: Semantic query
item.description:
Semantic query #

Semantic search with zero field knowledge: the vector field and the embedding model resolve from the collection schema, and the request is plain text — the retrieval question asked without naming a field, a model, or a vector.

Examples # 

POST /my-collection/_search
{"query": {"semantic": "find documents about search engines"}}

The clause composes inside bool like any other leaf — the text is embedded and the clause rewritten before execution:

item.title: Traverse query
item.description:
Traverse query #

Term and full-text queries match document content; none of them can ask “what is connected to these documents?” — the question citation graphs, reference data and knowledge graphs are made of. The traverse query answers it: a bounded graph traversal over a relation-typed edge field — starting from seed documents, walk the edges up to max_depth hops and emit every reached node as a hit.

Scores encode distance — 1.0 / (1.0 + depth) — so seeds outrank 1-hop neighbors, which outrank 2-hop neighbors, and the standard top-K collector orders the results.

item.title: Field collapsing
item.description:
Field collapsing #

Collapse the result list so each distinct value of a field appears at most once — “best product per merchant”, “best article per author” — without a terms aggregation, keeping full hit semantics (scores, source, highlight).

POST /my-collection/_search

How it works #

Collapse is engine-native and runs as a post-retrieval step. The collector normally stops at from + size, but collapse pages over GROUPS, so the engine first gathers a wider window — max(1000, from + size) hits (COLLAPSE_WINDOW in lib/engine/src/search/mod.rs) — in request sort order, then:

item.title: Fuzzy query
item.description:
Fuzzy query #

Returns documents that contain terms similar to the search term, within the maximum edit distance (Levenshtein — with transpositions counting as a single edit by default).

Use it when the indexed terms are only approximately known: typos in identifiers, OCR noise, or human-entered names.

Inside a nested query: not supported yet — the clause is rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause.

How it works #

The value is expanded against the inverted index’s term dictionary by edit distance, then the survivors’ postings are unioned like a should of term queries. The engine takes the union of three resolution passes — the value recorded as an exact term, a whole-value fuzzy walk, and (on non-keyword fields) a per-token walk after running the field’s search analyzer over the value — so the query works on keyword fields and on analyzed text alike (the per-token pass matters for CJK and multi-word input). On keyword fields the raw value is used, with the field’s normalizer applied first and no tokenization.

item.title: Geo-shape query
item.description:
Geo-shape query #

Matches documents whose geo_shape field relates to a query geometry by a spatial relation. The query geometry is a GeoJSON geometry object or a WKT string; the indexed shape was written the same way.

Where the geo_point queries ask “is this point inside my region?”, geo_shape asks it of whole geometries — the document carries a polygon, line or envelope (a delivery zone, a pipeline route, a parcel) and the query tests it against another geometry.

item.title: Graph projection block
item.description:
Graph projection block #

Add a graph block to any search request and the response carries a graph — nodes and edges — built from the hit set, alongside the normal hits. Where the traverse query searches by walking edges, the graph block renders: it takes the documents a query already found and projects them into a node/edge structure a UI (or a GraphRAG pipeline) can consume directly.

graph LR subgraph walk["traverse — searches by walking"] S("seeds") -->|"walk edges
up to max_depth"| H1["hits — every reached node,
scored by distance"] end subgraph render["graph — renders what was found"] Q("any query") --> H2("hit set") H2 -->|"project the relation field"| G["nodes + edges
for a UI or GraphRAG"] end

item.title: Lesson 5 — Graph traversal
item.description:
Lesson 5 — Graph traversal #

Relations are the first of the two features that most distinguish Pizza from a plain text index: edges as a first-class query target. This lesson walks edges inside one collection — the traversal sections run live in the browser widget, and the modeling section at the end is curl against a live node.

Graph queries are also the one lesson without a SQL pairing: traverse stays DSL-side — it is demand-gated outside the SQL M1 subset, which stops at the single-collection statement.

item.title: Max bucket aggregation
item.description:
Max bucket aggregation #

A sibling pipeline aggregation identifying the largest per-bucket metric value — e.g. the best-performing group. Bucket aggregations can sort their own output, but only inside one request’s bucket list; max_bucket lifts the winning number out as a single headline metric next to the breakdown.

"best_seller": { "max_bucket": { "buckets_path": "per_type>revenue" } }

How it works #

max_bucket is declared next to the bucket aggregation it consumes and runs after every regular aggregation — including the distributed merge — has finished. It walks the parent’s finished buckets, collects one number per bucket, and returns their maximum as a single-value metric ({"value": 1800}) placed alongside the parent. Only the value is returned — not which bucket produced it; read the parent’s bucket list (or sort it with bucket_sort) when you need the winner’s key.

item.title: Min aggregation
item.description:
Min aggregation #

A single-value metrics aggregation that keeps track and returns the minimum value among numeric values extracted from the aggregated documents. It answers “how low does this field go” over any query — the floor of a price range, the earliest timestamp in a window, the cheapest item that matches a filter.

How it works #

The engine walks the matching documents once, keeping the smallest value seen; any larger value costs one comparison. Values are coerced to doubles as they are read — integers, floats and booleans (true = 1, false = 0) qualify, non-numeric values such as keyword strings do not.

item.title: Query string query
item.description:
Query string query #

Returns documents that match a compact query-syntax string, e.g. status:active AND title:search. The same parser powers the URI search parameter ?q=.

Inside a nested query: not supported yet — the clause is rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause.

How it works #

The query string is parsed with the classic query-string grammar and converted to native queries: bare and field-qualified terms become analyzed match queries, quoted phrases become phrase queries, and the boolean operators become bool clauses. Terms without a field: prefix go to default_field (or, when fields is set, the query fans out into a bool.should across those fields with their field^boost weights). The operator subset:

item.title: Significant terms aggregation
item.description:
Significant terms aggregation #

A multi-bucket aggregation returning terms that are unusually frequent in the current scope (foreground) compared with the whole index (background) — the classic “what’s special about this subset” query.

In this engine significant_terms currently approximates that idea by foreground frequency: it ranks the scope’s values by their in-scope doc_count, without computing background statistics. Nest it under a query or a parent bucket to scope the foreground set; the values that dominate that scope come out on top.

item.title: Boolean query
item.description:
Boolean query #

A query that matches documents matching boolean combinations of other queries. It is built using one or more boolean clauses.

Inside a nested query: supported — must/filter/should/must_not and minimum_should_match all apply within ONE array element; clauses matched by different elements never combine.

How it works #

bool compiles each clause list into iterator algebra: must clauses intersect (AND), must_not clauses subtract, filter clauses intersect without scoring, and should clauses are probed per matched document — a streaming two-pointer walk that adds each matching should score on top of the base hit, with no intermediate materialization.

item.title: Lesson 6 — Hybrid search
item.description:
Lesson 6 — Hybrid search #

Most engines hide their fusion behind a magic flag. Pizza exposes the retrieval pipeline as explicit request stages — retrieve runs retrievers in parallel, fuse merges them, and two more stages re-shape scores afterwards:

retrieve → fuse → score_functions → rescore
(parallel (merge (function (second pass
 retrievers) the lists) scoring) on the top window)

Every stage is optional and combines with a plain query — you can use score_functions alone on a keyword search, or the full chain for hybrid retrieval.

item.title: Range aggregation
item.description:
Range aggregation #

A multi-bucket aggregation over numeric fields where each bucket is a user-defined range. It answers “how many documents fall in each band?” — the bands are yours to name and place, unlike the regular grid of histogram.

How it works #

Each range is a half-open window: from is inclusive, to is exclusive, and either side may be omitted for unbounded. A document whose value v satisfies from <= v < to counts in that range — and because the test is per range, overlapping definitions put one document in several buckets at once.

item.title: Stats bucket aggregation
item.description:
Stats bucket aggregation #

A sibling pipeline aggregation returning count/min/max/avg/sum of a metric across buckets — the stats of the per-bucket values. One call replaces four: where avg_bucket, min_bucket and max_bucket each reduce the bucket list to a single number, stats_bucket returns the whole summary object beside the aggregation it describes.

"day_stats": { "stats_bucket": { "buckets_path": "per_day>revenue" } }

How it works #

stats_bucket is declared next to the bucket aggregation it consumes and runs after every regular aggregation — including the distributed merge — has finished. It walks the parent’s finished buckets, collects one number per bucket, and emits the stats result object over that sample:

item.title: Streaming search
item.description:
Streaming #

Search on Pizza is real-time — documents are visible the moment they are written. The stream block attaches delivery directives to a search request: how the engine should pace and batch the emission of a result that outgrows one response, instead of making the client poll.

POST /my-collection/_search

How it works #

stream is a native, parsed block of the Pizza request DSL (StreamConfig in lib/engine/src/search/request/mod.rs) — accepted, validated, and carried through the engine with every request. Its knobs describe the emission strategy of the search pipeline:

item.title: Sum aggregation
item.description:
Sum aggregation #

A single-value metrics aggregation that sums up numeric values that are extracted from the aggregated documents. It turns “how much in total” into one number — revenue, bytes, durations, counts of units — without shipping the matching documents anywhere.

How it works #

The engine walks the matching documents once, adding each value to a running total. Values are coerced to doubles as they are read — integers, floats and booleans (true = 1, false = 0) contribute, non-numeric values such as keyword strings do not.

item.title: Wildcard query
item.description:
Wildcard query #

Returns documents that contain terms matching a wildcard pattern. The pattern supports * (any sequence of characters, including none) and ? (any single character).

Inside a nested query: not supported yet — the clause is rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause.

How it works #

The pattern is expanded against the inverted index’s term dictionary: the engine walks the field’s terms, keeps those matching the pattern, and unions their postings lists — the same result as a should of term queries over the surviving terms. Matching is anchored at both ends: web-1 is the whole term, so web-* matches web-10 and web-1 itself, but *web-1* is required for anything with text on both sides.

item.title: Date range aggregation
item.description:
Date range aggregation #

A multi-bucket aggregation like range, but for date fields. Each bucket is a from/to period you name — “before the launch”, “launch week”, “after” — which is the shape reporting questions naturally take, rather than the uniform grid of date_histogram.

How it works #

Bounds are epoch milliseconds: from accepts a number (or a numeric string) and is inclusive, to is exclusive, and either may be omitted for an open-ended period. Date strings like "2024-06-04" are not parsed by the aggregation — convert them to epoch millis first (the teaching examples below show the constants).

item.title: Extended stats bucket aggregation
item.description:
Extended stats bucket aggregation #

A sibling pipeline aggregation extending stats_bucket with variance, standard deviation and their sampling variants of the per-bucket metric distribution. Use it when the spread of the per-bucket numbers matters — how uneven the days or categories are — not just their min/avg/max envelope.

"day_xstats": {
 "extended_stats_bucket": { "buckets_path": "per_day>revenue" }
}

How it works #

extended_stats_bucket is declared next to the bucket aggregation it consumes and runs after every regular aggregation — including the distributed merge — has finished. It walks the parent’s finished buckets, collects one number per bucket, and emits an extended_stats-shaped result over that sample:

item.title: Lesson 7 — Geographic search
item.description:
Lesson 7 — Geographic search #

From schema to data to queries: filter documents by where they are — a coordinate, a rectangle, an arbitrary polygon, or a full geometric shape.

Pizza has two geographic field types, and picking the right one is the whole design step:

  • geo_point — a single coordinate. Answers “where is this document?” Distance, box and polygon filters run against it.
  • geo_shape — a full geometry: point, line, polygon, multi-variant, envelope or geometry collection. Answers “what area does this document cover?” and supports the relation vocabulary (intersects, within, contains, disjoint).

A store is a geo_point; the district it serves is a geo_shape.

item.title: Match all query
item.description:
Match all query #

Matches every document. This is the default query used when no query is sent in a search request — relevance-free, constant-scored, and the base every “everything, then narrow” pattern builds on.

How it works #
