match_all walks every document in the target indexes with a constant score — 1.0 — so _score carries no ranking information and downstream score arithmetic (indices_boost, bool should boosts, cross-engine merges) sees the same baseline everywhere. boost multiplies the constant, and is the only parameter there is.

item.title: Regexp query
item.description:
Regexp query #

Returns documents that contain terms matching a regular expression.

A regular expression is a way to match patterns in data using placeholder characters, called operators. For a list of operators supported by the regexp query, see Regular expression syntax. Use the regexp query when neither prefix, suffix nor wildcard can express the shape — alternation, character classes, repetition.

Inside a nested query: not supported yet — the clause is rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause.

item.title: Script fields
item.description:
Script fields #

Compute extra values for each hit, at fetch time, from the hit’s own _source — like highlighting, but producing numbers and strings instead of fragments. Scripts run on Pizza’s sandboxed script engine (see the script language reference), only for the hits actually returned on the page.

Every returned hit carries the computed values under fields, as arrays:

item.title: Value count aggregation
item.description:
Value count aggregation #

A single-value metrics aggregation that counts the number of values that are extracted from the aggregated documents. Typically, this aggregator will be used in conjunction with other single-value aggregations. For example, when computing the avg one might be interested in the number of values the average is computed over.

value_count does not de-duplicate values, so even if a field has duplicates each value will be counted individually.

item.title: Histogram aggregation
item.description:
Histogram aggregation #

A multi-bucket aggregation over numeric fields that applies a fixed interval to build the buckets. It answers “how are the values distributed?” — every document lands in exactly one bucket, and the bucket keys form a regular grid over the value axis.

How it works #

Each document’s value v is placed by index arithmetic — bucket index floor((v - offset) / interval) — so a bucket covers the half-open window [key, key + interval). Buckets accumulate in a sorted map, and the response lists them by ascending key.

item.title: Lesson 8 — Joins
item.description:
Lesson 8 — Joins #

Traversal (Lesson 5) walks edges inside ONE collection. A join spans TWO: it answers questions a single collection cannot — orders whose customer is gold-tier, where the tier lives in a different collection.

Joins need a running node (the gateway orchestrates the two sides, which is why the wasm playground does not host them), so this lesson is curl against your Lesson 1 node — no live widget. Like traverse, join stays DSL-side outside the SQL M1 subset.

item.title: Median absolute deviation aggregation
item.description:
Median absolute deviation aggregation #

A single-value metrics aggregation that computes the median absolute deviation — the median of the distances from each value to the median of all values. A robust measure of spread: unlike standard deviation it is not skewed by a few extreme values.

How it works #

The aggregation runs in three steps over the collected values of the field:

  1. Compute the median with the same TDigest arithmetic percentiles uses — weight-1 centroids at (i + 0.5) / n, linear interpolation between the two bracketing values.
  2. Take each value’s absolute distance to that median, |v − median|.
  3. Return the median of those distances, using the same arithmetic again.

Because both medians interpolate, the result can land between observed values (over the 120 teaching sale prices: median 22.5, MAD 7.5 — neither is a price anyone paid). The value is expressed in the same units as the field, so a MAD of 7.5 on prices means “a typical sale is $7.50 away from the median price”.

item.title: Percentiles bucket aggregation
item.description:
Percentiles bucket aggregation #

A sibling pipeline aggregation computing percentiles of a metric across buckets — e.g. “the daily-revenue p95”. The mean of the per-bucket values answers “what is typical”; percentiles answer “what the whole ladder of buckets looks like” — including the outlier end that a stats_bucket min/max flattens into two numbers.

"day_pcts": { "percentiles_bucket": { "buckets_path": "per_day>revenue" } }

How it works #

percentiles_bucket is declared next to the bucket aggregation it consumes and runs after every regular aggregation — including the distributed merge — has finished. It walks the parent’s finished buckets, collects one number per bucket, sorts them, and evaluates each requested percentile over the sorted sample, returning a {"values": {...}} object keyed by the percentile:

item.title: Span queries
item.description:
Span queries #

Span queries are low-level positional queries that expose and control the positions of terms — the building blocks for phrase-adjacent logic that phrase does not express directly. Most use cases are better served by match_phrase (or its slop); the span family exists for the remaining ones.

Inside a nested query: not supported yet — span clauses are rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause. Use phrase with slop for positional logic.

item.title: Suffix query
item.description:
Suffix query #

Returns documents that contain terms ending in the provided value. This is the mirror of the prefix query; like a leading wildcard, it is more expensive than a prefix match.

Inside a nested query: not supported yet — the clause is rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause.

How it works #

A term dictionary is sorted by its beginnings, so a prefix can seek directly to its subtree — but a suffix cannot. The engine therefore walks the whole dictionary of the field and keeps the terms that end with the value, then unions their postings lists exactly like a should of term queries. The cost is proportional to the number of distinct terms in the field, not to the number of matches, which is why the suffix query is marked more expensive than prefix.

item.title: Intervals query
item.description:
Intervals query #

The intervals query is a rule language for term positions: it matches documents whose analyzed token stream satisfies proximity rules you express as a tree — fixed token sequences, maximum gaps, required order, unions, multi-term leaves, and positional filters between sibling rules. It covers everything phrase expresses plus the shapes a phrase cannot: unordered combinations with bounded width, disjunctions of positional rules, and prefix/wildcard/fuzzy/regexp leaves inside positional composition.

item.title: Lesson 9 — Operations
item.description:
Lesson 9 — Operations #

Keeping a node healthy: partial updates in place, compaction, the change feed, and reading cluster state. This lesson is server-side — start a node as in Lesson 1 and run the curls against it.

The use case #

The features that matter once the node serves real traffic: mutating documents without rewriting them, keeping storage healthy, reacting to every write, and reading cluster state. The questions this lesson answers:

item.title: Range query
item.description:
Range query #

Returns documents that contain terms within a provided range.

Use it for intervals: prices between two numbers, events inside a time window, names inside an alphabetical span — anything expressible as “from / to” bounds rather than a list of exact values.

Inside a nested query: supported — the bounds apply per array element.

How it works #

The engine picks the index by field type:

item.title: Variable width histogram aggregation
item.description:
Variable width histogram aggregation #

A multi-bucket aggregation like histogram, but bucket edges adapt to the data so each bucket holds roughly the same number of documents. Fixed grids go blind where data is sparse and waste resolution where it is dense; the variable-width form spends its buckets where the documents actually are.

How it works #

The engine collects every numeric value, sorts it, and partitions the sorted run into buckets contiguous segments such that the sum of squared distances to each segment’s mean is minimal — the classic one-dimensional k-segmentation problem, solved exactly with dynamic programming and prefix sums (an O(1) cost function per candidate cut). When n × k exceeds 1,048,576 it falls back to equal-count chunking, a linear-time approximation. buckets is capped at the number of distinct values, so asking for more buckets than there are values simply yields one bucket per value.

item.title: Weighted average aggregation
item.description:
Weighted average aggregation #

A single-value metrics aggregation that computes the weighted average of numeric values. Each document contributes value × weight, divided by the total weight — e.g. an average price weighted by quantity sold. When documents are not all equally important, avg is the wrong tool and this is the right one.

How it works #

The engine walks the matching documents once, accumulating Σ(value × weight) in the numerator and Σ weight in the denominator; the result is their quotient. Both sides are computed in the same pass over two columns, so the pairing of a document’s value with its own weight is never lost.

item.title: Date histogram aggregation
item.description:
Date histogram aggregation #

This multi-bucket aggregation is similar to the normal histogram, but it can only be used with date fields. Dates are represented internally as epoch milliseconds, so the plain histogram can technically run on them too — but calendar intervals are not a fixed length (a month is 28–31 days), which is exactly what this aggregation handles.

How it works #

Date fields store epoch milliseconds at ingest, and the aggregation builds its grid on those numbers. calendar_interval and fixed_interval select between two grid types (exactly one must be set):

item.title: Exists query
item.description:
Exists query #

Returns documents that contain an indexed value for a specific field.

A document matches when the field has at least one non-null value — an empty string or an empty array does not count as existing.

Inside a nested query: supported — matches elements that carry the field.

How it works #

exists never touches the inverted index. It is answered from the stored-field / column layer, where every document either carries the key or does not:

item.title: Stats aggregation
item.description:
Stats aggregation #

A multi-value metrics aggregation that computes basic statistics (min, max, sum, count, avg) over numeric values extracted from the aggregated documents. It is avg, min, max and sum folded into one request — the five numbers most dashboards put side by side, for the price of one column scan.

How it works #

The engine walks the matching documents once, maintaining a running count, sum, minimum and maximum; avg is derived at the end as sum / count. Everything is exact — no sampling, no sketches. Values are coerced to doubles as they are read: integers, floats and booleans (true = 1, false = 0) contribute, non-numeric values such as keyword strings do not.

item.title: Auto date histogram aggregation
item.description:
Auto date histogram aggregation #

A multi-bucket aggregation like date_histogram, but you choose the NUMBER of buckets and the engine picks the interval that best fits. It solves the cold-start problem of time charts: when you do not know whether the data spans minutes or years, you state the resolution you want on screen and let the ladder decide the unit.

How it works #

The engine reads every date value (epoch milliseconds), takes the data extent max − min, and divides by the buckets target to get a rough per-bucket width. That width is matched against a fixed ladder, and the smallest interval that covers it wins: 1s, 1m, 5m, 10m, 30m, 1h, 6h, 12h, 1d, 1w as fixed intervals; beyond a week the calendar units month, quarter, year (and multi-year multiples for very long extents). The pick is one closed-form step, not an iterative search.

item.title: Extended stats aggregation
item.description:
Extended stats aggregation #

A multi-value metrics aggregation extending stats with squares, variance, standard deviation and their lower/upper bounds. Where stats says what the values are, extended_stats says how tightly they cluster around the mean — the input for outlier bands, quality gates and anything else built on “how unusual is this value”.

How it works #

The engine walks the matching documents once, maintaining a running count, sum, sum_of_squares, minimum and maximum — the same single pass as stats, plus one multiply-add for the squares. Everything downstream is derived from these raw moments, and is exact (no sampling, no sketches):

item.title: Derivative aggregation
item.description:
Derivative aggregation #

A parent pipeline aggregation computing the difference between each bucket’s metric and the previous bucket’s — “how much did it change”. A time series says where you are; the derivative says which way and how fast you are moving, bucket by bucket. The first bucket has no predecessor and answers null.

"delta": { "derivative": { "buckets_path": "revenue" } }

How it works #

derivative is declared inside the multi-bucket aggregation it decorates (the parent style), next to the metric it consumes. After the buckets are built, the engine walks them in order and attaches current − previous to each bucket under the pipeline’s own name:

item.title: Fetch a document
item.description:
Fetch a document #

Retrieve an existing document by specifying its unique identifier.

Examples #

Fetch a document from the my-collection collection with customized uuid news_001:

GET /my-collection/_doc/news_001

The API returns the following result:

{
 "_collection": "default:my-collection",
 "_id": "0,0",
 "_key" : "news_001",
 "found": true,
 "source" : {
 "message": "GET /search HTTP/1.1 200 1070000",
 "org": {
 "id": "infini"
 }
 }
}

As you can see, the customized uuid are represented as _key within the document, and there is also a _id returned with value 0,0, this is the internal id generated by Pizza, and it is guaranteed to be unique, so you can also fetch this document by this value like this:

item.title: IP range aggregation
item.description:
IP range aggregation #

A multi-bucket aggregation like range, but for IP addresses — buckets are CIDR masks or from/to IP bounds. It answers network-shape questions: which subnet does this traffic belong to, and how much of it is in the private ranges versus the internet.

How it works #

The field’s string values are parsed into 128-bit numbers, with IPv4 mapped into the IPv6 space as ::ffff:a.b.c.d — an order-preserving numeric comparison. From/to buckets are half-open on that number (from inclusive, to exclusive), so IPv4 and IPv6 bounds interoperate; 10.0.0.0 sorts before 192.168.0.0 sorts before 2001:db8::.

item.title: More like this query
item.description:
More like this query #

more_like_this finds documents similar to given text or documents. The engine extracts the input’s terms, keeps the significant ones, and runs the resulting top terms as a disjunctive query — a “find more of this” query without any embedding model.

fields is required and limited to text fields.

How it works #

The query is rewritten at the search entry point — it is a client of the analysis and term pipeline, not an index structure. Per field: gather the like text (free text is analyzed with the first field’s analyzer; a referenced document contributes the text of every query field), tokenize it, drop terms below min_term_freq, outside the word-length bounds, or listed in stop_words, and remove every term the unlike inputs produced. The surviving terms from all fields are pooled, ranked by source term frequency (ties broken alphabetically for determinism), and the top max_query_terms become a bool.should of term queries governed by minimum_should_match. If nothing survives, the query matches nothing. When include is false (the default) and the like input named documents, their ids are added as a must_not — the seed documents trivially contain every selected term.

item.title: Percentiles aggregation
item.description:
Percentiles aggregation #

A multi-value metrics aggregation that calculates one or more percentiles over numeric values extracted from the aggregated documents.

Percentiles show the point at which a certain percentage of observed values occur. For example, the 95th percentile is the value which is greater than 95% of the observed values.

Percentiles are often used to find outliers. In normal distributions, the 0.13th and 99.87th percentiles represents three standard deviations from the mean. Any data which falls outside three standard deviations is often considered an anomaly.

item.title: Cumulative sum aggregation
item.description:
Cumulative sum aggregation #

A parent pipeline aggregation adding a running total column to each bucket — the metric plus every earlier bucket’s. A histogram says what each period brought in; the cumulative sum says where the whole span stands at every point along it, without a second query or client-side arithmetic.

"running": { "cumulative_sum": { "buckets_path": "revenue" } }

How it works #

cumulative_sum is declared inside the multi-bucket aggregation it decorates, next to the metric it consumes. After the buckets are built, the engine walks them in order and attaches the running total to each bucket under the pipeline’s own name:

item.title: Filter aggregation
item.description:
Filter aggregation #

A single-bucket aggregation that narrows the documents a nested aggregation runs on, with a query acting as the filter condition. Where the request’s query scopes everything, filter carves out one named sub-scope inside the aggregation tree — the aggregation equivalent of a WHERE clause.

How it works #

Every matching document is tested against the condition; those that pass form the bucket. The response is a single-bucket object carrying the filtered doc_count plus any nested aggregation results:

item.title: Percentile ranks aggregation
item.description:
Percentile ranks aggregation #

A multi-value metrics aggregation that answers the inverse of percentiles: for each value you provide, what percentage of documents is at or below it.

How it works #

The engine collects every value of the field and sorts it once. For each requested value v, the rank is the fraction of collected values that are less than or equal to v:

rank(v) = count(value <= v) / n * 100

The comparison is inclusive — a document exactly at v counts toward its own rank, so the rank of the maximum value is 100, not 100 − 1/n. With no values at all (empty result set, or every document missing the field) each rank is null.

item.title: Boxplot aggregation
item.description:
Boxplot aggregation #

A multi-value metrics aggregation producing the five-number summary of a distribution: minimum, lower quartile (q1), median (q2), upper quartile (q3) and maximum, plus whiskers.

How it works #

The engine collects and sorts the values of the field, then:

  • min / max are the observed extremes (after missing substitution).
  • q1, q2, q3 are the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles, computed with the same TDigest arithmetic percentiles uses — weight-1 centroids at (i + 0.5) / n with linear interpolation between the two bracketing values. A quartile can therefore land between observed values (q2 of the sale prices is 22.5, between 15 and 30).
  • The whiskers extend from the quartiles by 1.5 × IQR, where IQR = q3 − q1, and are clamped to the data: lower = max(q1 − 1.5·IQR, min), upper = min(q3 + 1.5·IQR, max). Values beyond the unclamped whisker positions are the conventional boxplot outliers.

Clamping means on a compact distribution the whiskers simply touch the extremes — over the teaching sales prices the whiskers land exactly on min and max. If no document has a value for the field, all seven numbers are 0.

item.title: Cumulative cardinality aggregation
item.description:
Cumulative cardinality aggregation #

A parent pipeline aggregation reporting a running total of a per-bucket distinct count — typically a cardinality metric — answering “how many unique values have been counted up to and including each bucket”.

"seen_so_far": {
 "cumulative_cardinality": { "buckets_path": "buyers" }
}

How it works #

cumulative_cardinality is declared inside the multi-bucket aggregation it decorates, next to the metric it consumes. The engine walks the finished buckets in order and attaches the running total of the referenced values under the pipeline’s own name — mechanically the same accumulation as cumulative_sum; only the intended input (a per-bucket distinct count) differs.

item.title: Filters aggregation
item.description:
Filters aggregation #

A multi-bucket aggregation where each bucket is defined by a named filter — all filters run over the same document set, giving per-filter counts (and nested sub-aggregations) side by side. It is the aggregation form of a KPI panel: one request, several named slices.

How it works #

The filters object maps bucket names to query clauses. Every matching document is tested against EVERY filter independently, so buckets may overlap — a document counts toward each filter it satisfies, and toward none when it satisfies none. Bucket counts therefore do not sum to the hit total in general.

item.title: Adjacency matrix aggregation
item.description:
Adjacency matrix aggregation #

A multi-bucket aggregation returning every named filter’s document set plus their pairwise INTERSECTIONS — the cross product view of several filters. Where filters answers each filter separately, this one also tells you how much they overlap, which is exactly what co-occurrence analysis needs.

How it works #

Each named filter is evaluated against every candidate document, so a document can carry several filter flags at once. The engine then emits one bucket per non-empty filter (keyed by its name) and one bucket per non-empty pair, keyed a&b with the two names in alphabetical order. Intersections beyond pairs — no a&b&c triples — are not computed, and empty buckets are skipped entirely, so the bucket count tops out at n·(n−1)/2 + n.

item.title: Serial diff aggregation
item.description:
Serial diff aggregation #

A parent pipeline aggregation computing the difference between each bucket’s metric and the bucket lag positions back — a differencing transform that turns a trending or seasonal series into its own period-over-period change.

"wowl": { "serial_diff": { "buckets_path": "revenue", "lag": 2 } }

How it works #

serial_diff is declared inside the multi-bucket aggregation it decorates, next to the metric it consumes. After the buckets are built, the engine walks them in order and attaches current − value_lag_buckets_back to each bucket under the pipeline’s own name:

item.title: String stats aggregation
item.description:
String stats aggregation #

A multi-value metrics aggregation computing length and character statistics over keyword/string values: count, min/max/avg length and Shannon entropy of the character distribution.

How it works #

Every document that has a string value for the field contributes one string. Over those strings the engine reports:

  • count — how many values were seen (documents without the field are skipped, not counted);
  • min_length, max_length, avg_length — length statistics in UTF-8 bytes, so a non-ASCII character counts as its encoded width;
  • entropy — Shannon entropy of the pooled character frequencies, in bits: -Σ p(c) · log2 p(c) over the share p(c) of each character across all strings. Constant text gives 0; text where every character is equally likely gives log2(alphabet size).

The character frequencies are pooled across all contributing values before the entropy is taken, so repetition across documents counts: the teaching type field repeats the same few words 120 times and still scores ≈3.22 bits.

item.title: Global aggregation
item.description:
Global aggregation #

A single-bucket aggregation whose nested aggregations run over all documents in the search context, ignoring the query scope. It is the baseline column of every analytic table: “this slice” next to “the whole dataset”, computed in the same request instead of a second round-trip.

How it works #

Normally an aggregation sees only the documents the query matched. global detaches its sub-aggregations from that scope: the engine takes the exact set of live documents — visibility and tombstones honored, per segment — and aggregates over that instead. The result is one bucket shaped { "doc_count": <all live docs>, …sub-aggs }; the aggregation itself takes no parameters beyond its sub-aggregations.

item.title: Matrix stats aggregation
item.description:
Matrix stats aggregation #

A multi-value metrics aggregation computing counts, means, variances, skewness, kurtosis and the correlation matrix across several numeric fields at once.

How it works #

The aggregation works row-wise: a document contributes a row only if it has a value for every listed field (a missing map can fill gaps per field). Documents with any gap are dropped entirely — the reported count is the number of complete rows, and every statistic uses the same rows. At least two rows are required; below that the result is empty.

item.title: Moving fn aggregation
item.description:
Moving fn aggregation #

A parent pipeline aggregation computing a window statistic over the last N buckets’ metrics — MovingFunctions.max(values), MovingFunctions.sum(values), MovingFunctions.min(values) and friends, with the window sliding bucket by bucket.

"smooth": {
 "moving_fn": {
 "buckets_path": "revenue",
 "window": 3,
 "script": "MovingFunctions.max(values)"
 }
}

How it works #

moving_fn is declared inside the multi-bucket aggregation it decorates, next to the metric it consumes. After the buckets are built, the engine slides a trailing window over their values and, for each bucket, evaluates the script once with the window exposed as values — a floating-point array, oldest first, current bucket last. The script’s numeric result is attached to that bucket under the pipeline’s own name.

item.title: Missing aggregation
item.description:
Missing aggregation #

A single-bucket aggregation of the documents that have no indexed value for a field — the inverse of the exists query. It turns data gaps into a number you can alert on, instead of discovering them when a report quietly undercounts.

How it works #

For every document the query matched, the engine checks whether the field has an indexed value in the column store — an absent field and an explicit null both count as missing. The matching documents form one bucket shaped { "doc_count": N, …sub-aggs }; sub-aggregations run over exactly those incomplete documents, so you can ask not just how many rows are broken but how they break.

item.title: Moving avg aggregation
item.description:
Moving avg aggregation #

A parent pipeline aggregation smoothing a metric with a moving average over the last N buckets — one averaged point per bucket, flattening noise so the trend underneath shows.

"smooth": {
 "moving_avg": { "buckets_path": "per_day>revenue", "window": 3 }
}

How it works #

In this engine moving_avg is evaluated in the sibling placement: declare it next to the bucket aggregation and point buckets_path at the series with the full parent>metric form. After the buckets are built, the engine slides a trailing window over their values and emits a standalone buckets array (keys 0..n−1) with one value per consumed bucket — the average of the window ending at that bucket.

item.title: Replace a document
item.description:
Replace a document #

Replace an existing document by specifying its unique identifier and the new content.

Examples #

Replace a document news_001 of the collection my-collection with new content:

PUT /my-collection/_doc/news_001
{
 "message": "GET /search HTTP/1.1 200 1070000",
 "org": {
 "id": "infinilabs"
 }
}

The API returns as following result:

{"_id":"0,0", "_key":"news_001", "result":"updated"}

After the document modification, If you perform the fetch request:

GET /my-collection/_doc/news_001

It returns an updated document like:

{
 "_collection": "default:my-collection",
 "_id": "0,0",
 "_key" : "news_001",
 "found": true,
 "source" : {
 "message": "GET /search HTTP/1.1 200 1070000",
 "org": {
 "id": "infinilabs"
 }
 }
}

The replacement happens in place: the document keeps its original _id, and the index entries of the old version are rebuilt under the same _id. Since this is a full replacement, fields that are omitted from the request body are cleared.

item.title: T-test aggregation
item.description:
T-test aggregation #

A single-value metrics aggregation for a Student’s t-test over two numeric fields. Positive values mean a tends to be larger than b.

How it works #

The engine collects every value of a.field and every value of b.field across the bucket’s documents — the two samples grow independently, so a document missing one field still contributes to the other sample — and computes Welch’s two-sample t-statistic:

item.title: Bucket script aggregation
item.description:
Bucket script aggregation #

A parent pipeline aggregation computing arithmetic on a bucket’s own metrics — the script references sibling metrics by name through params and its result becomes a new per-bucket value. It is the SQL SELECT a / b AS c of the aggregation world: one derived column, evaluated once per bucket over values the bucket already holds.

"avg_order": {
 "bucket_script": {
 "buckets_path": { "r": "revenue", "n": "orders" },
 "script": "params.r / params.n"
 }
}

How it works #

bucket_script is declared inside the multi-bucket aggregation it decorates, next to the metrics it consumes. After the buckets are built, the engine resolves each named path against every bucket, binds the numbers into the script’s scope, evaluates the script once, and inserts its result under the pipeline’s own name — the response shape buckets[i].avg_order.value.

item.title: Rate aggregation
item.description:
Rate aggregation #

A single-value metrics aggregation that reduces a numeric field inside date_histogram buckets (per-interval totals), intended for counters that accumulate over time.

How it works #

rate reads one field and reduces it per bucket, with three reduction modes selected by mode:

  • sum (default) — the bucket’s total of the field; identical to sum.
  • value_count — how many values the field has in the bucket.
  • avg — the bucket’s mean of the field.

If field is omitted entirely, the aggregation counts the documents in the bucket (the value_count shape over _doc).

item.title: Sampler aggregation
item.description:
Sampler aggregation #

A single-bucket aggregation that keeps only a sample of the matching documents before running its sub-aggregations — used to cut aggregation cost on very large result sets. If a terms aggregation over millions of documents is too slow or too memory-hungry, sampling trades exact counts for an order-of-magnitude answer at a fraction of the cost.

How it works #

The sampler keeps the first shard_size matching documents (default 100) and discards the rest; its sub-aggregations then run over that sample only. The result is a single bucket keyed sample, carrying the sample’s doc_count and the sub-aggregation results:

item.title: Bucket selector aggregation
item.description:
Bucket selector aggregation #

A parent pipeline aggregation filtering the bucket list itself: a script predicate per bucket — buckets whose script evaluates false are dropped from the response. It is the HAVING clause of the aggregation world: the predicate sees computed metrics, not documents.

"big_days": {
 "bucket_selector": {
 "buckets_path": { "r": "revenue" },
 "script": "params.r > 150"
 }
}

How it works #

bucket_selector is declared inside the multi-bucket aggregation it decorates, next to the metrics it consumes. After the buckets are built, the engine resolves each named path against every bucket, evaluates the script once as a boolean, and removes the buckets that fail from the owning aggregation’s response. The selector itself never appears in the output — it is a filter, not a metric.

item.title: Diversified sampler aggregation
item.description:
Diversified sampler aggregation #

Like sampler, but the sample is diversified by a field — up to one (or few) documents per value — so rare categories survive the sampling. A plain sampler can be flooded by the most common value (every sampled type being t-shirt); the diversified variant guarantees representation for every distinct value first.

How it works #

The sampler walks the matching documents in two passes. First it caps each distinct value of the diversify field at max_docs_per_value (default 1) — extra documents with an already-full value are dropped. Documents missing the diversify field share one common group. The survivors are then sorted and truncated to the overall shard_size (default 100).

item.title: Geo bounds aggregation
item.description:
Geo bounds aggregation #

A metrics aggregation computing the bounding box (top-left / bottom-right corners) of all geo_point values — the rectangle that just contains every point in the bucket.

How it works #

The engine scans the bucket’s geo_point column, tracks the minimum and maximum latitude and longitude, and emits:

{
 "bounds": {
 "top_left": { "lat": <max lat>, "lon": <min lon> },
 "bottom_right": { "lat": <min lat>, "lon": <max lon> }
 }
}

null when the bucket holds no parseable point. The column-store fast path and the executor path run the same min/max scan.

item.title: Partial update a document
item.description:
Partial update a document #

Sometimes we may only need to update a portion of the fields of a document. A partial update fetches the stored document, merges the partial doc body, applies the ordered ops operators, and replaces the document in place under its original _id — the new values are visible to search immediately.

Examples #

Update the org.id field of the document with system id 0,0 in the collection my-collection:

item.title: Bucket sort aggregation
item.description:
Bucket sort aggregation #

A parent pipeline aggregation sorting (and paginating) the bucket list by any of the bucket’s metrics — the pipeline counterpart of the request-level sort.

"by_revenue": {
 "bucket_sort": { "sort": [ { "revenue": { "order": "asc" } } ] }
}

How it works #

Status, verified against the engine: bucket_sort is accepted but not yet active. The request parses — sort, from and size are accepted — but no reordering or truncation is applied: the parent aggregation’s buckets come back in the parent’s own order. A declared bucket_sort evaluates to a null metric, and nested declarations currently leave a "by_revenue": { "value": null } placeholder in each bucket (unlike bucket_selector, it does not clean up after itself).

item.title: Geo centroid aggregation
item.description:
Geo centroid aggregation #

A metrics aggregation computing the centroid (mean latitude and longitude) of all geo_point values.

How it works #

The engine sums latitudes and longitudes across the bucket’s geo_point values and divides by the count:

{
 "location": { "lat": .., "lon": .. },
 "count": 15
}
  • The mean is arithmetic per axis (a planar average, not spherical) — exact enough at city or country scale, drifting only for extents that cross the 180th meridian or span hemispheres.
  • Every parseable point counts once; there is no weight field. The result is null when the bucket holds no points.
  • Under distributed fan-out the coordinator keeps its own shard’s value (geo metrics have no mergeable intermediate), so single-node results are the exact ones.
  • Like every geo_point consumer, the aggregation sees points normalized at ingestion: {"lat": .., "lon": ..}, [lon, lat] (longitude first) or a "lat,lon" string, all stored as two-dimensional BKD points.

Examples #

Returns the count of points and their centroid — the natural center point for map placement. Over the 15 places: count: 15, location about {lat 31.7484, lon 111.2181}.

item.title: Geo distance aggregation
item.description:
Geo distance aggregation #

A multi-bucket aggregation like range, but buckets are distance rings around a geo_point origin. It answers “how many things are near me?” — counts per radius band in a single request, no matter how many rings you declare.

How it works #

Every document’s point is measured against the origin with the haversine formula on a spherical Earth (mean radius 6,371,008.8 m — within ~0.5 % of the WGS-84 ellipsoid). The origin accepts either a "lat,lon" string or a { "lat": …, "lon": … } object; an origin that parses to nothing yields zero buckets.

item.title: Reshard a rolling
item.description:
Reshard a rolling #

Change the number of shards of a rolling, online. Splitting raises the shard count (finer partition ranges, e.g. 1 → 2); merging lowers it (e.g. 2 → 1).

The reshard builds a hidden target rolling while the source keeps serving every read and write. Existing documents are streamed into the target with their _id preserved, the write tail is replayed until the target converges, and a single metadata commit then swaps the target in atomically. Documents stay addressable under the same _id and _key throughout, including for writes issued while the reshard is building.

item.title: Geohash grid aggregation
item.description:
Geohash grid aggregation #

A multi-bucket aggregation that groups geo_point values into geohash cells — the building block of map clustering. It answers “where are my documents concentrated?” in one request, handing the map a count per cell instead of thousands of individual markers.

How it works #

Each document’s point is encoded as a geohash string: base-32 characters produced by interleaving longitude and latitude bits over successively halved intervals. precision is the number of characters kept — 1–12, clamped, default 5 (cells of roughly 4.9 km × 4.9 km). The classic Amsterdam coordinate 52.374081, 4.912350 at precision 3 lands in cell u17.

item.title: Normalize aggregation
item.description:
Normalize aggregation #

A parent pipeline aggregation rescaling a bucket metric into a share or rank — e.g. each bucket’s revenue as a percent of the total (percent_of_sum), a 0..1 position (rescale_0_1), or standard deviations from the mean (z-score).

"share": {
 "normalize": { "buckets_path": "per_type>revenue", "method": "percent_of_sum" }
}

How it works #

In this engine normalize is evaluated in the sibling placement: declare it next to the bucket aggregation and point buckets_path at the series with the full parent>metric form. The engine collects one value per bucket, applies the chosen method across the whole series, and emits a standalone buckets array (keys 0..n−1) with one value per consumed bucket.

item.title: Salting (salt-split routing)
item.description:
Salting (salt-split routing) #

Manage salt-split assignments for a collection whose schema declares a routing field ("routing": true). One hot routing value — the mega tenant, the biggest org — funnels every write into a single partition; salting splits that value across a SET of partitions so the hot key stops being a placement bottleneck.

The API never moves data by itself: assignments state intent, the write path consumes them live (the very next write of an assigned value lands inside its partition set), and migrating documents that are already placed is a separate rehash operation. The joins tutorial walks the complete sequence against a live node.

item.title: Top hits aggregation
item.description:
Top hits aggregation #

Keeps track of the most relevant documents being aggregated — useful inside a bucket aggregation (e.g. terms) to return the best-matching documents per bucket. Where most metric aggs reduce a bucket to one number, top_hits keeps the documents themselves.

How it works #

top_hits runs over a bucket’s document set and returns up to size documents in a hits envelope: hits.total — a plain count of the bucket’s documents — and hits.hits[], each entry carrying _id (the engine’s internal numeric document id) and _source.

item.title: Delete a document
item.description:
Delete a document #

Delete a specific document from the specified collection by specifying its unique identifier.

Examples #

Delete the document 0,0 from collection my-collection:

DELETE /my-collection/_doc/0,0

The API returns the following result:

{
 "_id": "0,0",
 "_version": 0,
 "result": "deleted",
 ...
}

Deleting a document again (or fetching it after deletion) answers 404 with "result": "not_found" — the delete itself still succeeds and reports "result": "deleted" only for a document that was live.

item.title: Geotile grid aggregation
item.description:
Geotile grid aggregation #

A multi-bucket aggregation grouping geo_point values into zoom/x/y map tiles — the native grid of web maps. Where geohash_grid speaks in geohash strings, this one emits exactly the tile addresses a Leaflet/MapLibre layer already understands, so clustering needs no coordinate translation.

How it works #

Each point is mapped to its Web-Mercator tile: x and y are computed from longitude/latitude scaled by 2^zoom, latitude clamped to the projection’s ±85.0511° limit. precision is the zoom level — 0–29, default 7 (a tile spans ~300 km at the equator; each zoom step halves it). The bucket key is the z/x/y string, e.g. Amsterdam at zoom 8 → 8/131/84.

item.title: Scripted queries
item.description:
Scripted queries #

Scripts in the search request: script_score to compute the score, a script predicate in a boolean filter, and a _script sort key. All run on Pizza’s sandboxed script engine (see the script language reference) — Rhai, not Painless, but the doc['x'].value, _score, params.<name> spellings run unmodified.

script_score — score by script #

Wrap a query; the script’s value replaces the score. The script sees _score (the wrapped query’s BM25 score), doc (the hit’s _source in doc-values shape) and params:

item.title: Top metrics aggregation
item.description:
Top metrics aggregation #

A metrics aggregation that returns metric values from the leading matching documents — a cheaper alternative to top_hits when you only need field values, not whole documents.

Engine note: sort is accepted for compatibility; the current implementation returns the metrics of the first size matching documents.

How it works #

top_metrics walks the bucket’s documents and emits one entry per document for the first size of them, in index order. Each entry maps every configured metric field to its value in that document. The response is the flat form {"top": [{"price": 15.0}, …]}.

item.title: Nested aggregation
item.description:
Nested aggregation #

A single-bucket aggregation that scopes its sub-aggregations to a nested object path. Nested field values are addressable as dotted columns, so sub-aggregations read variants.color style fields directly — counting per array element where it matters, not per parent document.

reverse_nested (only valid inside a nested aggregation) jumps back out to the parent-document scope.

How it works #

The engine returns a single bucket shaped { "doc_count": <parents>, …sub-aggs }. Sub-aggregations run over the parent documents, but the nested path’s values live in multivalue dotted columns, so a terms on variants.color buckets every array ELEMENT: over the 30 teaching products with 60 variant elements, black / white / blue each collect 20. One exception is top_hits, which is element-level here: each hit is one stored element carrying _nested: {field, offset} identity, sorted per the requested sort.

item.title: Pipeline scripts
item.description:
Pipeline scripts #

Three pipeline aggregations evaluate a user-supplied script per bucket: bucket_script (compute a new metric per bucket), bucket_selector (keep/drop predicate), and moving_fn (window statistic). moving_avg is a moving_fn with a fixed averaging script. The same engine powers scripted_metric (scripts per document instead of per bucket) and the scripted value sources on the single-value metric aggs (sum, avg, min, max, value_count, cardinality), the per-hit script_fields of a search request (fetch phase), and the scripted queries — script_score, script filters, the _script sort.

item.title: Rescore
item.description:
Rescore #

rescore re-ranks the top window of hits with a second query — an expensive precision pass (phrase, vector similarity, a narrow filter match) applied only where it can change the final page, instead of to every matching document.

POST /my-collection/_search

How it works #

Rescore is engine-native. When a request carries a rescore block, the collector widens its gather to max(from + size, window) candidates, the first-pass query ranks them, and the store layer then applies the rescore to the collected set (apply_rescore_to_result in lib/engine/src/store/layered/generic_reader.rs, blending in lib/engine/src/search/scorer/mod.rs):

item.title: Scripted metric aggregation
item.description:
Scripted metric aggregation #

A metrics aggregation whose result is computed by your own scripts, in four phases, running on Pizza’s sandboxed script engine (see the script language reference).

How it works #

One state map per segment, folded once at the end:

Phase Runs Scope
init_script once per segment state, params
map_script once per document state, doc, params
combine_script once per segment state, params
reduce_script once, at the end states, params

state is a map you own — initialize it in init_script, accumulate into it in map_script. combine_script folds one segment’s state into a single value (a script that ends in a statement returns the state itself, the default when combine_script is omitted). reduce_script receives all combined values as the states array; if it is omitted, a single state passes through unchanged and several come back as an array — the parts, rather than a wrong merge. Builds without the scripting feature return null for the whole aggregation.

item.title: Children aggregation
item.description:
Children aggregation #

A single-bucket aggregation that scopes its sub-aggregations to the child documents of a relation field (parent-child joins). In a corpus where parents and children share an index, it is the lens that looks at the child side while the outer query talks about parents.

How it works #

Engine note: the current implementation runs sub-aggregations over the scoped document set keyed by the relation; it does not resolve per-parent child sets.

item.title: Composite aggregation
item.description:
Composite aggregation #

Paginated multi-source bucket aggregation: the composite key is a tuple built from several sources (a terms field, a histogram interval, a date_histogram, a geotile_grid), and pages are pulled with an after cursor. It does what a single terms cannot: group by several dimensions at once, and stream all combinations without oversizing size.

How it works #

Each entry in sources is named: { "day": { … } } binds day to one dimension of the composite key. A bucket’s key maps each source name to its value; buckets come back in ascending key order — first source most significant, values compared as numbers when both are (numbers sort before strings), as strings otherwise.

item.title: Batch document operation
item.description:
Batch document operation #

Provides a efficient way to perform multiple index, create, delete, and update operations in a single request.

Examples # 

POST /_bulk
{ "index" : { "_index" : "test", "_id" : "1" } }
{ "field1" : "value1" }
{ "delete" : { "_index" : "test", "_id" : "2" } }
{ "create" : { "_index" : "test", "_id" : "3" } }
{ "field1" : "value3" }
{ "update" : {"_id" : "1", "_index" : "test"} }
{ "doc" : {"field2" : "value2"} }

The API returns the following result:

{
 "took": 30,
 "errors": false,
 "items": [
 {
 "index": {
 "_collection": "default:test",
 "_id": "0,0",
 "result": "created",
 ...
 }
 },
 {
 "delete": {
 "_collection": "default:test",
 "_id": "0,1",
 "result": "not_found",
 ...
 }
 },
 {
 "create": {
 "_collection": "default:test",
 "_id": "0,2",
 "result": "created",
 ...
 }
 },
 {
 "update": {
 "_collection": "default:test",
 "_id": "0,0",
 "result": "updated",
 ...
 }
 }
 ]
}

Request # 

POST /_bulk
POST /<target>/_bulk

Path parameters #

  • <target>
    (Optional, string) Name of the collection to target. Actions that don’t explicitly specify their target in the action line use it.

Query parameters #

  • realtime
    (Optional, boolean, default: true) Request-level write-mode switch that overrides schema property-level realtime settings for every document in this request: false applies the batch WAL-only (durable immediately, searchable after the offline epoch build).
  • key_as_id
    (Optional, boolean, default: false) compatibility rendering: keyed documents answer with the user key AS _id (see the index API).
  • sync_replication
    (Optional, boolean) Opt back into synchronous inline replication for this request (wait for the replica RPC and count it in the response).

item.title: Change feed (CDC)
item.description:
Change feed (CDC) #

GET /_changes serves a collection’s change log tail from the shard engines’ WALs, so external systems can replicate Pizza data elsewhere — off-site disaster recovery, secondary indexing, audit pipelines — with a standard poll loop:

GET /demo:orders/_changes?since=abc:3,def:1&limit=1000

{
 "results": [
 {"shard":"abc…","rolling_id":0,"epoch_id":4,"seq":0,
 "id":"0,7","key":"u1","op":"create","doc":{"qty":3}},
 {"shard":"abc…","rolling_id":0,"epoch_id":4,"seq":1,
 "id":"0,8","op":"delete"}
 ],
 "cursors": {"abc…": 4, "def…": 1},
 "purged_below": {"abc…": 3},
 "active": {"abc…": 5},
 "pending": true
}

Request # 

GET /_changes
GET /<targets>/_changes

Path parameters #

  • targets
    (Optional, string) Comma-separated collection names (wildcard supported); the target-less form feeds every collection.

Query parameters #

  • since
    (Optional, string) Per-shard epoch cursors from a previous response, shard_hex:epoch,shard_hex:epoch. Omit to start from the beginning of the retained tail.
  • limit
    (Optional, integer) Maximum rows to return. Defaults to 1000.

Consuming the feed #

  1. Poll with the cursors of the previous response as the next since (persist the cursors — they are the checkpoint).
  2. pending: true means more rows exist beyond limit; poll again immediately, otherwise poll at your cadence.
  3. Compare each cursor against purged_below: a cursor below that floor means the WAL retention window (wal.local.retention_epoch / retention_bytes) has already purged part of the tail for that shard. The tail is incomplete — run a full resync (search + re-bulk into the DR cluster) and resume from the current cursors.
